title: Weight and mass: why a balance works on the Moon and a spring scale does not

summary.text: A shopkeeper's two-pan balance would give the same answer on the Moon, but a spring scale would not. Your child finds out why by building both kinds of scale from a rubber band, a ruler and cups of water, where 100 millilitres of water has a mass of 100 grams. They hang cardboard shapes from a plumb line to find where a thing's weight seems to pull, and they weigh a bottle before and after it fizzes to see where mass goes. They then learn how the Earth itself was weighed, and what its weight showed about its inside.
summary.art: A two-pan balance and a rubber band scale side by side on a kitchen table, with cups of water, a lemon, and a small Moon drawn above.

intro.hook: In a shop in Madurai, a mango sits in one pan of a two-pan balance. A 300-gram weight sits in the other pan. The pans are level. Now take the same balance, the same mango and the same weight to the Moon, where things weigh about six times less. Will the pans still be level? And what if the shopkeeper uses a spring scale instead? Make a guess, and say why.
intro.text: A balance and a spring scale both give a number for a mango, but they do it in different ways. In this unit you build both from things at home. You find out how far a rubber band stretches as you add water, and how to turn that into a scale. You find the one point where a cardboard shape balances, which can be a point with no cardboard at all. You weigh a fizzing bottle to see where mass goes. And you find out how, more than 200 years ago, someone weighed the whole Earth.
intro.art: A mango in one pan and a 300-gram weight in the other pan of a brass balance, with the Moon in the sky behind the shop.

outcomes: I can explain that a balance compares masses, so it gives the same answer on the Moon, while a spring scale measures a pull, so it gives a different answer.
I can build a scale from a rubber band, calibrate it with water, and use my graph to find an unknown mass.
I can say that the stretch of a spring or band grows with the load, and that a band is not as steady as a steel spring.
I can work out the weight of something on another world from its mass and the pull of that world in newtons for each kilogram.
I can find the centre of gravity of a flat shape with a plumb line, and say why it can lie outside the shape.
I can explain why a low, wide thing is hard to topple, using the centre of gravity.
I can show with a scale that mass is not lost when things dissolve, melt or fizz, and say where it goes.
I can tell how Henry Cavendish weighed the Earth, and what it showed about the inside of the Earth.

terms.meaning: A scale with two pans that compares one mass with another. When the pans are level, the two masses are equal.
terms.example: A shopkeeper puts a mango in one pan and a 300-gram weight in the other. When the pans are level, the mango has a mass of 300 grams.
terms.art: A brass two-pan balance with a mango in one pan and a weight in the other, and a pointer in the middle.

terms.meaning: A scale with a spring inside. The spring stretches by an amount that shows the pull on it.
terms.example: A hanging scale in a vegetable shop shows the weight of a bag of tomatoes with a pointer.
terms.art: A hanging spring scale with a bag of tomatoes and a pointer moving along a dial.

terms.meaning: A mass that everyone agrees on and uses to check other scales. One litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram.
terms.example: A shopkeeper's iron one-kilogram weight is a standard mass.
terms.art: A brass one-kilogram weight beside a litre bottle of water, with an equals sign between them.

terms.meaning: To mark a scale by checking it against known masses, so its readings can be trusted.
terms.example: You hang 100, 200 and 300 millilitres of water on a rubber band and mark where the pointer sits each time.
terms.art: A rubber band with a ruler behind it and marks for 100, 200 and 300 grams.

terms.meaning: How much longer a band or spring becomes when you pull it. It is the new length minus the old length.
terms.example: A rubber band 7 centimetres long that stretches to 10 centimetres has a stretch of 3 centimetres.
terms.art: A rubber band at rest and the same band stretched, with a ruler showing the extra length.

terms.meaning: For a spring, the stretch grows evenly with the pull, up to a limit. Twice the pull gives twice the stretch. Robert Hooke wrote it in the 1670s.
terms.example: A steel spring that stretches 2 centimetres under 1 newton stretches 4 centimetres under 2 newtons.
terms.art: A spring hanging with one, two and three weights, and stretch marks growing in equal steps.

terms.meaning: The point past which a stretched band or spring does not spring back to its old length.
terms.example: If you pull a paper clip open too far, it stays bent.
terms.art: A paper clip bent open and staying bent, beside a spring that returns.

terms.meaning: The strength of a world's pull, which tells how many newtons of weight each kilogram has there. On Earth it is about 9.8.
terms.example: On the Moon the number is about 1.6, so a 1-kilogram bag weighs 1.6 newtons there.
terms.art: A table of worlds with Earth, Moon and Mars, each with its number of newtons for each kilogram.

terms.meaning: The one point where the whole weight of a thing seems to act. A thing balances if it is held up at this point.
terms.example: A ruler balances on your finger at its middle, which is its centre of gravity.
terms.art: A ruler balanced on a finger, with a small dot marking the centre and a downward arrow from it.

terms.meaning: A weight hanging on a thread. It points straight down, towards the centre of the Earth.
terms.example: A mason uses a plumb line to check that a wall is upright.
terms.art: A mason's thread with a stone hanging beside a brick wall.

terms.meaning: Hard to topple. A thing is stable when it has a low centre of gravity and a wide base.
terms.example: A steel bucket on the floor is stable. A tall stack of plates is not.
terms.art: A wide low pot and a tall narrow vase on a table, the pot with a firm tick and the vase tilting.

terms.meaning: To tip over. A thing topples when its centre of gravity moves past the edge of its base.
terms.example: A bus with luggage piled on the roof can topple on a sharp bend.
terms.art: A tilted bus with a vertical line from its centre of gravity falling outside its wheels.

terms.meaning: How much a thing resists a change in its movement. A thing with more mass has more inertia.
terms.example: A loaded handcart is harder to start and harder to stop than an empty one.
terms.art: A man pushing an empty cart and a woman struggling to push a cart piled with sacks.

terms.meaning: How much mass a material packs into a given space. Iron is dense. Cotton is not.
terms.example: A fist-sized lump of iron has much more mass than a fist-sized ball of cotton.
terms.art: A small iron ball and a large cotton ball on the two pans of a balance, with the iron pan lower.

terms.meaning: In a closed container, the total mass stays the same when things dissolve, melt or react. Nothing is lost. It only moves into another form.
terms.example: A sealed bag of ice has the same mass after the ice melts.
terms.art: A sealed bag on a scale before and after its ice melts, with the same number on the display.

terms.meaning: A tiny pattern of thin metal wire stuck to a part. When the part bends or stretches, the wire's electrical resistance changes. A digital scale uses it to sense a push.
terms.example: A bathroom scale has strain gauges inside, which feel the bending of the metal under your feet.
terms.art: A close-up of a small metal grid on a bar that bends, with wires going to a display.

terms.meaning: The heavy centre of a planet. The Earth's core is mostly iron and nickel, and holds about a third of the Earth's mass.
terms.example: Scientists know about the Earth's core from the way earthquake waves pass through the Earth.
terms.art: A cut-away of the Earth showing a crust, a mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

terms.meaning: The point that two bodies, such as the Earth and the Moon, both circle round. It is called the barycentre. It lies on the line between them, nearer the heavier one.
terms.example: The balance point of the Earth and the Moon lies inside the Earth, about 4,700 kilometres from its centre.
terms.art: The Earth and the Moon joined by a line, with a dot inside the Earth where the two orbits balance.

terms.meaning: A unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms.
terms.example: A small car has a mass of about one tonne.
terms.art: A small car on a weighbridge showing 1 tonne.

explanations.concept: A balance compares, so it works anywhere
explanations.definition: A two-pan balance compares two masses. When the pans are level, the two masses are equal. It gives the same answer on the Earth, on the Moon and in a lift.
explanations.description: On each pan, gravity pulls down on whatever is there. The pull on the left pan and the pull on the right pan are both made by the same world, so they change together. If the two masses are equal, the two pulls are equal at any place. If the pulls were six times smaller on the Moon, both would be six times smaller, and the pans would still be level. So a balance does not measure gravity at all. It measures how much stuff, which is mass. The mango and the 300-gram weight would balance on the Moon too. This is the way that shops have weighed things for thousands of years.
examples: A shopkeeper's tarazu, a two-pan balance with iron weights, gives the same answer in Kochi, on a mountain, or on the Moon.
A kilo of rice balances a kilo of iron on a balance anywhere, even though the rice takes up about ten times more room.
A goldsmith's tiny balance weighs gold the same way, by comparing it with small standard weights.
explanations.art: A two-pan balance on Earth and on the Moon, level in both pictures, with arrows showing the pull on each pan.

explanations.concept: A spring scale measures a pull, so the place matters
explanations.definition: A spring scale measures the pull on its spring. On the Moon, the same mango pulls about six times less, so a spring scale shows about six times less.
explanations.description: A spring scale does not compare the mango with a weight. It lets the mango stretch a spring, and reads the stretch. The stretch depends on how hard the mango is pulled down, which is its weight. On the Earth the pull on a 300-gram mango is about 3 newtons. On the Moon it is about 0.5 newtons. The mango has not lost any matter. The Moon simply pulls less. Many bathroom scales and kitchen scales also measure a push or a pull inside, then show a number in kilograms by assuming the Earth's pull. On the Moon, they would show about one sixth of the right mass.
examples: A hanging scale in a vegetable shop is a spring scale.
A digital kitchen scale that shows 500 grams on Earth would show about 80 grams for the same bag on the Moon.
A forcemeter in a school laboratory is a spring scale marked in newtons.
explanations.art: A mango on a spring scale on Earth showing 3 newtons and on the Moon showing 0.5 newtons.

explanations.concept: Hooke's law: the stretch grows evenly with the pull
explanations.definition: For a steel spring, the stretch grows evenly with the pull. Twice the pull gives twice the stretch. This holds until the elastic limit.
explanations.description: Robert Hooke, an English scientist, studied springs for clocks in the 1600s. He wrote in 1678 that the stretch is in proportion to the force. A spring scale is built on this. If a 100-gram load stretches a steel spring by 1 centimetre, a 200-gram load stretches it by 2 and a 300-gram load by 3. Marks on the scale are then evenly spaced. Past the elastic limit, the spring stays stretched, and the scale is spoilt. A rubber band is less steady than steel. It softens at first and stiffens later, so its line on a graph may bend. That is why you should always calibrate a homemade scale with known masses before you trust it.
examples: A paper clip opened a little springs back. Opened too far, it stays bent. That is the elastic limit.
A pen spring stretches evenly. A rubber band stretches less evenly.
A weighing scale in a vegetable shop has evenly spaced marks, because its spring follows Hooke's law.
explanations.art: A graph with stretch along the bottom and load up the side, showing a straight line for a spring and a bent line for a rubber band.

explanations.concept: How strongly a world pulls: newtons for each kilogram
explanations.definition: The pull of a world on each kilogram is its strength of gravity, in newtons for each kilogram. On Earth it is about 9.8.
explanations.description: On Earth, a mass of 1 kilogram has a weight of about 9.8 newtons. On the Moon it is about 1.6. On Mars it is about 3.7. On Venus it is about 8.9. At the cloud tops of Jupiter it is about 25. At the surface of the Sun it is about 274. These numbers depend on the mass of the world and on how far you are from its centre. The same number tells how fast a falling thing speeds up each second. Earth's 9.8 newtons for each kilogram goes with 9.8 metres per second more each second. Strong worlds pull hard and speed things up fast.
examples: On the Moon, a bag of 1 kilogram weighs 1.6 newtons. On Earth it would take only about 160 grams to weigh that much.
On Mars, the pull is about 3.7 newtons for each kilogram, a bit more than a third of Earth's.
At the surface of the Sun, a bag of 1 kilogram would weigh about 274 newtons, which is what a 28-kilogram bag weighs on Earth.
explanations.art: A table of six worlds with their pull in newtons for each kilogram, and a small bag shown on each.

explanations.concept: Weight equals mass times the pull of the world
explanations.definition: Weight in newtons equals mass in kilograms times the pull of the world in newtons for each kilogram.
explanations.description: A child of 30 kilograms on Earth has a weight of 30 times 9.8, which is 294 newtons. On the Moon it is 30 times 1.6, which is 48 newtons. On Mars it is 30 times 3.7, which is 111 newtons. Her mass is 30 kilograms in every place, because she brings all her matter with her. To feel what the Moon is like, you could carry a bag with a mass of about 160 grams in place of 1 kilogram. It pulls on your hand with the same force that 1 kilogram would on the Moon. This is why astronauts hop so easily on the Moon.
examples: On Earth, 30 kilograms weighs 294 newtons. On the Moon the same child weighs 48 newtons.
A 2-kilogram bag on Mars would feel like a bag of about 760 grams on Earth.
A 1-kilogram bag on Jupiter would feel like a bag of about 2.5 kilograms on Earth.
explanations.art: Three children of the same size, labelled Earth, Moon and Mars, each with a different weight in newtons and the same mass of 30 kilograms.

explanations.concept: The centre of gravity: one point for all the weight
explanations.definition: The centre of gravity is the one point where the whole weight of a thing seems to act. A thing balances if it is held up at this point.
explanations.description: Gravity pulls on every part of a thing, every crumb of cardboard and every grain of rice. You can add up all these pulls, and they act as if they were one pull at one point. That point is the centre of gravity. If you hang a shape from a pin, the shape swings until its centre of gravity is directly below the pin. A plumb line hung from the pin passes through it. Hang the shape from two or three different holes, and the plumb lines cross at the centre of gravity. For a ruler, it is in the middle. For a ring, it is in the empty hole. For a banana or a boomerang, it is in the air beside the shape.
examples: A ruler balances on a finger at its middle. A crescent of cardboard balances at a point in the air, in the bend of the crescent.
A tumbler toy such as a Thanjavur dancing doll rocks and comes upright, because most of its mass is in the base.
A high jumper who arches their back can pass over the bar while their centre of gravity passes under it.
explanations.art: A cardboard ring, a crescent and a blob, each hanging from a pin, with plumb lines crossing at a dot, and the dot for the ring in the middle of the hole.

explanations.concept: Steady or toppling: low, wide and over the feet
explanations.definition: A thing topples when a vertical line down from its centre of gravity falls outside its base. A low centre of gravity and a wide base make a thing stable.
explanations.description: Tilt a box slowly. At first, the line down from its centre of gravity still falls inside the base, and the box tips back. When the line passes the edge, the box falls over. A wide base makes the edge far away, and a low centre of gravity means you must tilt it a long way. That is why a steel bucket is steady and a tall vase is not. It is why a bus with luggage on the roof is dangerous, and why a lorry with a tall load can topple on a bend. You stay up by keeping the line down from your centre of gravity over your feet. Walking is falling forwards and catching yourself again.
examples: A bullock cart with sacks piled high is easier to topple than one with the sacks low.
A person carrying a pot on the head keeps the pot's centre of gravity directly over their neck.
A cricket bat stood on one end falls over easily, but a bat lying flat cannot fall at all.
explanations.art: A bus tilted on a bend with a plumb line from its centre of gravity falling outside the wheels, and a low wide bucket tilted but safe.

explanations.concept: Heavy things are hard to start and hard to stop
explanations.definition: Mass is also how much a thing resists a change in its movement. A thing with twice the mass needs twice the push to speed up in the same way. This is called inertia.
explanations.description: A full handcart is harder to get moving than an empty one, and harder to stop. The same push gives it a smaller change in speed. This does not depend on gravity. In space, where nothing weighs anything, a heavy crate is still hard to shove. Astronauts have to push hard to move a heavy crate, even though it floats. So mass does two jobs. It sets how hard gravity pulls on a thing, and it sets how hard the thing is to speed up. Scientists have found that these two jobs always match, and nobody knows why. This is why heavy and light things fall together.
examples: A cricket ball is harder to catch than a tennis ball moving at the same speed, because stopping a bigger mass needs a bigger push.
A loaded truck takes much longer to stop than an empty one.
An astronaut in orbit still needs a hard push to move a heavy crate, even though it weighs nothing.
explanations.art: An empty handcart and a loaded handcart, with the same-sized arrow for a push and a short and a long arrow for the speed gained.

explanations.concept: Mass is not lost: dissolving, melting, fizzing
explanations.definition: In a closed container, the total mass stays the same when sugar dissolves, ice melts or a bottle fizzes. Nothing is lost. Mass only moves into another form.
explanations.description: Stir sugar into water, and it seems to vanish. Weigh the cup before and after, and the mass is the same. Melt ice in a sealed bag, and the mass is the same. Mix baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bottle, and the mass is the same, even though gas has been made. Open the bottle, and the mass drops, because the gas floats away. Gas has mass too. Antoine Lavoisier, a French scientist, showed this carefully in the 1770s and 1780s, by weighing things before and after they changed inside sealed glass. His wife Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier drew his equipment, kept his notes and translated papers for him. A burning candle also does not vanish. Its wax turns into carbon dioxide and water vapour, which weigh just as much as the wax and the oxygen they came from.
examples: Sugar in tea does not vanish. The tea has the mass of the tea plus the sugar.
A burning candle gets lighter, because its wax leaves as invisible gases.
Rust makes an iron nail heavier, because the iron joins with oxygen from the air.
explanations.art: A sealed bottle on a scale before and after fizzing, with the same number, and an open cup on a scale where the number drops.

explanations.concept: Where does a tree's mass come from?
explanations.definition: Most of the dry mass of a plant comes from carbon dioxide in the air and from water, not from the soil.
explanations.description: In the first half of the 1600s, a Flemish doctor named Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a pot of soil for five years, and gave the tree only rainwater. The willow grew from about 2 kilograms to about 77 kilograms. The soil, dried and weighed again, had lost only about 57 grams. He decided the tree's mass came from water. Today we know the picture is fuller. In sunlight, leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and join it with water to make sugars. The carbon in the wood, in the leaves and in your food was once air. So a tree is built mostly out of air and water, with a little from the soil. Your own body gives its carbon back to the air each time you breathe out.
examples: Van Helmont's willow gained about 75 kilograms while the soil in the pot lost almost nothing.
A seed in a pot of soil grows into a plant with much more mass than the seed.
The carbon in a chapati was carbon dioxide in the air once, taken in by a wheat plant.
explanations.art: A willow tree in a pot with arrows of air and water going in and a small arrow of soil going in, and a balance showing the soil nearly unchanged.

explanations.concept: Weighing the Earth, and looking inside it
explanations.definition: The Earth has a mass of about 6 followed by 24 zeros, in kilograms. It is about 5.5 times as dense as water, which shows that its inside is much denser than its rocks.
explanations.description: In 1798, Henry Cavendish in England hung two small lead balls on a rod from a thin wire. He brought two big lead balls close. The small balls moved a tiny amount, because every mass pulls every other mass. From that tiny twist, he found the Earth's density. It was about 5.4 times that of water. Rock at the surface is only about 2.7 times as dense. So the inside of the Earth must be much heavier than its rocks. Today we know there is a core of iron and nickel. In 1936, a Danish scientist named Inge Lehmann studied earthquake waves and worked out that inside the liquid outer core there is a solid inner core. Nobody has dug deeper than about 12 kilometres. We know the rest from weighing and from waves.
examples: A cubic centimetre of average Earth has a mass of about 5.5 grams, a cubic centimetre of granite about 2.7 grams, and a cubic centimetre of water 1 gram.
The core of the Earth holds about a third of the Earth's mass.
Earthquake waves bend and speed up in the core, which is how Inge Lehmann found the solid inner core.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the Earth showing rock on the outside and a large iron core in the middle, and a torsion balance with two lead balls in the corner of the picture.

explanations.concept: How scales and the kilogram work today
explanations.definition: A digital scale senses a push with strain gauges. The kilogram is now defined from a fixed number in nature, and no longer from a metal cylinder.
explanations.description: A digital bathroom or kitchen scale has strain gauges inside. These are thin metal patterns whose electrical resistance changes when a bar bends a tiny amount under your weight. A small computer turns the change into a number. Because it feels a push, it shows the right mass only on Earth. For 130 years, the kilogram was a small cylinder of platinum and iridium, kept in a vault near Paris. Copies were sent to countries around the world. On 20 May 2019, the kilogram was redefined using a fixed value of the Planck constant, a number from quantum physics. A machine called a Kibble balance can now make the kilogram from electricity and the pull of gravity.
examples: A bathroom scale checks the push on it, and shows kilograms by assuming Earth's pull.
Many countries had copies of the old kilogram cylinder, and India's national standards of measurement are kept at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi.
A litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram. The kilogram was first meant to match a litre of water.
explanations.art: A bathroom scale cut open to show a metal bar with a small grid of wire on it, and a cylinder in a glass bell jar beside it.

explanations.concept: Big G: the number scientists cannot agree on
explanations.definition: Big G is the number in Newton's rule for gravity that sets how strongly any two masses pull each other. It is the least well known of the main constants.
explanations.description: Henry Cavendish's experiment can be redone with better tools. Laboratories around the world have measured big G, and their answers differ slightly, by more than the errors they claim. We know G to about 4 or 5 digits. Many other constants are known to eight or nine digits or more. Nobody knows why G is so hard to pin down. Gravity is extremely weak, so tiny stray pulls from nearby objects, from the weather, even from the people moving in the building, can spoil a measurement.
examples: Some other constants are known to nine digits or more. Big G is known to only about five.
Some experiments use two small masses hanging on a wire, as Cavendish did. Others use swinging pendulums or atoms.
A tiny lump of lead on the other side of a laboratory can change the result.
explanations.art: A laboratory with a torsion balance inside a glass case, and a scientist looking at a laser dot on the wall.

perspectives.explanation: The differences are hidden mistakes in the experiments, such as small stray pulls and tiny changes in the wire. With better tools, the answers will come together.
The differences may be real, and be a clue to something new about gravity. Nobody has shown this, and most scientists think it is unlikely.

agreed.text: A two-pan balance gives the same answer wherever you take it, but a spring scale does not.
agreed.evidence: On Earth, a balance reads the same on a mountain top and at sea level, while a very sensitive spring scale reads very slightly less on the mountain. The same reasoning holds on the Moon.

agreed.text: For a steel spring, the stretch grows evenly with the pull, up to a limit.
agreed.evidence: Robert Hooke wrote it in 1678, and spring scales have been built on it ever since. You can check it by hanging 100, 200 and 300 grams and measuring.

agreed.text: Weight equals mass times the pull of the world, in newtons for each kilogram.
agreed.evidence: The pull has been measured on Earth with pendulums and falling things, and on the Moon and Mars from the way spacecraft move round and land on them.

agreed.text: A thing's weight acts through its centre of gravity, which can lie outside the thing.
agreed.evidence: Hang any shape from several points and the plumb lines cross at one place. For a ring or a crescent, that place is in empty space.

agreed.text: In a closed container, the total mass stays the same when things dissolve, melt or react.
agreed.evidence: Lavoisier showed it in the 1770s and 1780s. In 1908, Hans Landolt checked it with sealed vessels and found no change larger than about one part in ten million.

agreed.text: The Earth is about 5.5 times as dense as water, and it has a core of iron and nickel.
agreed.evidence: Cavendish weighed the Earth in 1798 with lead balls. Later scientists found the core from the way earthquake waves bend and speed up as they pass through the Earth.

challenging.claim: A balance and a spring scale measure the same thing.
challenging.who: Many people, because both give a number in kilograms in a shop on Earth.
challenging.for: In a shop on Earth, a balance and a spring scale give the same number for a mango.
challenging.against: A balance compares two masses and does not depend on how hard the world pulls. A spring scale measures the pull itself. On the Moon, the balance gives the same answer and the spring scale gives about one sixth of it.

challenging.claim: The centre of gravity is a spot in the middle of a thing, inside the material.
challenging.for: For a ruler or a ball, the centre of gravity is in the middle, inside the material.
challenging.against: For a ring, it is in the empty hole. For a crescent, a boomerang or a person bending over, it lies in the air beside the shape. It is a point we find by adding up all the pulls, not a part of the material.

challenging.claim: When something burns or dissolves, some of its mass disappears.
challenging.who: Many people, and natural philosophers before the 1700s.
challenging.for: A burnt candle is smaller, and sugar in tea cannot be seen.
challenging.against: Lavoisier weighed things in sealed vessels before and after burning, and the total never changed. The mass moves into gases and solutions. If the container is open, gas floats away, and the scale shows a drop.

challenging.claim: A plant's mass comes from the soil.
challenging.who: Aristotle, an ancient Greek thinker, and many people since.
challenging.for: Roots go into the soil, and plants grow only where there is soil.
challenging.against: Van Helmont's willow grew about 75 kilograms in five years while the soil in the pot lost only about 57 grams. Most of a plant's dry mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, and from water.

challenging.claim: The Earth is solid rock all the way through.
challenging.for: Every rock we can dig up is rock, and the surface looks like rock everywhere.
challenging.against: The Earth's average density, found by Cavendish in 1798, is about 5.4 times that of water. Surface rock is only about 2.7 times. So the inside must be much denser. Earthquake waves later showed an iron core, with a solid inner core found by Inge Lehmann in 1936.

challenging.claim: Big G is known exactly, so the strength of gravity between any two masses is certain.
challenging.who: Many people, who see it printed in tables.
challenging.for: The number is printed to many digits in tables, and gravity behaves very regularly.
challenging.against: Careful laboratories get answers that differ by more than they should. Big G is known to only about five digits. Gravity is so weak that tiny stray pulls spoil the measurements.

big_questions.q: A balance works on the Moon, and a spring scale does not. Which one tells you how much of a thing there really is?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one needs from the world in order to work.

big_questions.q: Your centre of gravity can be in the air, outside your body, when you bend over. Where is 'you' then?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the centre of gravity is a part of you or a point that we work out.

big_questions.q: The centre of gravity is a point we work out by adding up all the pulls, and may have nothing in it. Is it real? What other useful things are only worked out, such as the average height of a class?
big_questions.hint: Is the average height of a class a real child?

big_questions.q: In a sealed bottle, the mass stays the same even when gas appears from nothing you can see. What does that tell you about gas?
big_questions.hint: Think about what gas is made of, and what happened when you opened the cap.

big_questions.q: A tree is built mostly from air and water. Where does a tree end and the air begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the carbon in a chapati, and where it was before it was in the wheat.

big_questions.q: The Earth and the Moon both circle a point inside the Earth. Is the Moon circling the Earth, or are they circling each other?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Earth wobbling a little as the Moon goes round.

big_questions.q: Everyone who buys and sells by weight must trust the weights. Who decides what a kilogram is, and why should everyone trust them?
big_questions.hint: Think about the market, inspectors, and a standard that every country agrees on.

big_questions.q: A heavy thing is hard to lift and also hard to push sideways in space. Are these two facts about mass really the same fact?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your arm is doing in each case, and what gravity has to do with it.

big_questions.q: We weighed the Earth without ever going inside it. What else do we know about by weighing and watching, but never seeing directly?

story.title: The Litre of Water in the Spice Market
story.note: A made-up story. Zainaba, Ummamma, Mr Joseph and Seema Teacher are imagined. The Mattancherry spice market in Kochi is real, and traders there really did use balances with iron weights. The science is true: a litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram, a two-pan balance compares masses, and a digital kitchen scale has to be checked against a known mass. In real life, a good kitchen scale reads very close to the right value, but a cheap or damaged one can be off.
text: The spice market in Mattancherry, in Kochi, wakes before the sun. By six in the morning, the lanes smell of pepper and cloves, dried ginger and cardamom. Sacks lean against each other like tired people at a bus stop.
Ummamma's stall stood at the corner of the third lane. She had sold pepper there for fifty years. On her counter sat a brass balance with two shallow pans and a row of iron weights, black with age.

Her granddaughter Zainaba was ten, and she was allowed to put the weights on the pan. 'The kilo goes on the left,' Ummamma always said. 'The pepper goes on the right. Then you wait, and watch the pointer, until it stands still.'
One morning, a man came to the stall with a face like a monsoon sky. He was Mr Joseph, a retired bank clerk who lived near the church. In his hand was a shiny new kitchen scale.
'Yesterday I bought a kilo of your pepper,' he said. 'At home, I weighed it on this. Nine hundred and sixty grams. Forty grams short!' He set the scale on the counter like evidence in a court.
Ummamma went very still. 'Fifty years,' she said quietly. 'In fifty years, no one has said this to me.' Her hand shook on the brass pan. 'I have never cheated anyone.'

Zainaba looked at the grey iron weights, and then at the shiny scale. She thought of Seema Teacher at school, who had said: 'A number on a scale is only as good as the scale. Before you trust it, check it against something you already know.'
'Mr Joseph,' she said, 'may I try your scale?' He frowned at a girl who was ten years old, but he nodded.

She took an empty water bottle from under the counter. She stood it on his scale and pressed the little button that made the number go to zero. Then she filled the bottle at the stall's tap, right up to the one-litre line.

'A litre of water,' said Zainaba, 'has a mass of one kilogram. That is how the kilogram began. Everyone knows it, even the people who made your scale.' She set the bottle back on the pan. The numbers flickered, and settled. Nine hundred and sixty-two.

Mr Joseph stared at them. 'It says nine hundred and sixty-two.' 'Yes,' said Zainaba. 'My bottle holds a kilo of water, and your scale says it is nearly forty grams short. Forty grams short is just what it said about the pepper.'

'Perhaps your water is short too,' said Mr Joseph, but his voice had gone small. 'Then let us ask Ummamma's balance,' said Zainaba. She put the iron kilo weight in the left pan, with an empty bottle exactly like the other one beside it. In the right pan, she put the bottle of water. The two empty bottles cancelled out each other. The pointer swayed, steadied, and stood straight up.

'The iron kilo and the water kilo agree with each other,' she said. 'It is only your scale that disagrees. Ummamma's balance does not know how hard the Earth pulls. It only compares one thing with another, so it would give the same answer on the Moon. Your scale has to turn a push into grams, and somebody has to set that right.'

Mr Joseph turned the scale over, as if the answer might be written underneath. 'Perhaps the battery is weak,' he said at last. 'Perhaps it was never set right.' 'Perhaps,' said Zainaba kindly. 'It does not matter why. What matters is this. Before you trust a scale, weigh something you already know.'
Ummamma's eyes were wet. She put a kilo of pepper on the right pan, and the pointer stood straight up, as it had for fifty years.
Mr Joseph bowed his head to the old woman. 'I owe you an apology.' Ummamma waved her hand, as if brushing away a fly. 'Buy some cardamom,' she said. 'It has no apologies in it.'

The next week, he came back with the scale in one hand and a bottle of water in the other. 'Every morning now, I check it before I weigh anything,' he told Zainaba. 'My wife says I have become a scientist.'
'Everyone who weighs things is a scientist,' said Zainaba, and she handed him a paper cone of cardamom, which weighed exactly what it was supposed to.
story.epiphany: Before you trust a scale, weigh something you already know, such as a litre of water. A balance only compares one mass with another, so it gives the same answer anywhere. A scale that turns a push into grams has to be checked.
ask: Why did Zainaba weigh a litre of water on Mr Joseph's scale, instead of the pepper?
Why did she put an empty bottle in the left pan, beside the iron weight?
Why would Ummamma's balance give the same answer on the Moon, but Mr Joseph's scale would not?
How could you check a kitchen scale at home without any weights?

games.title: Moon Market: same on the Moon, or different?
games.context: This is a card game about mass and weight. Each card describes something you could measure or do. Players decide if it would give the same answer on the Moon, or a different one, and then say why.

setup.art: A pile of cut-out cards, a row of world cards and eight round tokens on a table, with a pencil and a score sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Make a pile of cards and a row of world cards.

setup.art: A reader holding a card and three players each placing a token face down, either Same or Different.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone places a token face down.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together, and the reader showing the back of the card with the answer and the reason.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the answer on the back.

printables.title: 24 situation cards to cut out (the situation on the front, the answer and the reason on the back)

items.f: A two-pan balance shows a mango level with a 300-gram weight.
items.b: Same on the Moon. Both pans are pulled equally, so a balance gives the same answer anywhere.

items.f: A spring scale shows 3 newtons for the same mango.
items.b: Different. The Moon pulls about six times less, so the scale would show about 0.5 newtons.

items.f: The mass of a bag of rice, 2 kilograms.
items.b: Same on the Moon. Mass is how much rice there is, and the bag brings all of it.

items.f: The weight of that same bag of rice.
items.b: Different. It is about 20 newtons on Earth and about 3 newtons on the Moon.

items.f: The reading of a digital kitchen scale for 500 grams of sugar.
items.b: Different. It senses the push and assumes Earth's pull, so it would show only about 80 grams.

items.f: The number of grains of rice in the bag.
items.b: Same on the Moon. Counting grains does not depend on gravity.

items.f: How hard it is to lift a full bucket of water.
items.b: Different. The bucket pulls on your arm about six times less.

items.f: How hard it is to stop a fast cricket ball.
items.b: Same on the Moon. Stopping a moving ball depends on its mass and its speed, not on its weight.

items.f: The balance point of a cardboard ring.
items.b: Same on the Moon. It depends on the shape of the ring, not on how hard the world pulls.

items.f: The angle at which a tall vase tips over.
items.b: Same on the Moon. It depends on where the centre of gravity is over the base, though the vase would fall more slowly.

items.f: The stretch of a rubber band with a mango hanging from it.
items.b: Different. The mango pulls the band about six times less on the Moon, so it stretches less.

items.f: The amount of matter in your body.
items.b: Same on the Moon. You carry all of your matter with you.

items.f: How high you can jump with the same push from your legs.
items.b: Different. About six times higher, because gravity pulls you back more slowly.

items.f: The mass of a shopkeeper's iron one-kilogram weight.
items.b: Same on the Moon. It is still 1 kilogram of iron.

items.f: What a bathroom scale shows when you stand on it, in kilograms.
items.b: Different. It would show only about one sixth of your mass.

items.f: A seesaw balanced with two children of equal mass.
items.b: Same on the Moon. The pull on each child falls by the same amount, so they still balance.

items.f: How long a pendulum takes to swing once.
items.b: Different. With less pull, it swings back more slowly, about 2.5 times as long.

items.f: The size of the dent a ball makes in dough when it is dropped.
items.b: Different. On the Moon the ball falls more slowly and hits softly.

items.f: The mass of a litre of water.
items.b: Same on the Moon. It is still about 1 kilogram of water.

items.f: The weight of an astronaut wearing a heavy space suit.
items.b: Different. On the Moon the total is about one sixth of the weight on Earth.

items.f: A cardboard shape hanging from a pin with its centre of gravity directly below the pin.
items.b: Same on the Moon. The shape swings until its centre of gravity is below the pin, there too.

items.f: The weight of a child whose mass is 30 kilograms.
items.b: Different. About 294 newtons on Earth and about 48 newtons on the Moon.

items.f: The sugar in a cup of tea.
items.b: Same on the Moon. Sugar does not change with the world.

items.f: How fast a dropped pencil reaches the floor.
items.b: Different. It falls more slowly on the Moon, so it takes longer to land.
