printables.title: 8 tokens: four that say Same on the Moon, and four that say Different on the Moon

rules: Make one pile of the 24 situation cards, with the situation side up. Lay the 8 world cards in a row, with the world side up.
Each player takes one Same token and one Different token. If there are fewer than four players, each player may take two of each.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
A right pick scores 1 point. A player who also says why in one sentence, using mass, weight, pull or push, scores 1 more point.
The reader turns over the card and reads the back to check. Then the next player becomes the reader.

After every third card, the reader picks a world card and says a mass, for example 10 kilograms. Everyone works out the weight on that world, by multiplying the mass by the number on the back of the world card. The right answer scores 2 points.
Play until all 24 cards are used. The most points wins. If you play alone, play both parts and try to beat 40 points.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 situation cards, the 8 world cards and the 8 tokens. Put the situation cards in a pile. Lay the world cards in a row.
flow.say: Each card describes something we could measure on Earth. We will decide if it would give the same answer on the Moon, or a different one.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Make a pile. Lay the world cards in a row.
flow.parent: Remind your child that the Moon pulls about one sixth as hard as the Earth. A thing's mass stays the same there, but its weight goes down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Moon Market. You set up the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Play a practice turn with the card about the two-pan balance. Place tokens, turn them over together, and read the back.
flow.say: Practice turn. A balance shows a mango level with a 300-gram weight. On the Moon, will the pans still be level? Why?
flow.kid: A balance on the Moon. Same, or different? Why?

check.q: A balance shows a mango level with a 300-gram weight. On the Moon, what will the pans do?
options: Stay level, because both pans are pulled less by the same amount
Tip towards the weight, because the Moon pulls less on the mango
Float up, because there is no air
check.why: Both pans lose the same fraction of their pull, so they stay level. Picking the second answer forgets that the weight is pulled less too.

flow.context: In this step, you play a practice turn and learn how to pick a token.

flow.do: Play the game. After every third card, the reader picks a world card and says a mass for everyone to work out the weight.
flow.say: Reader, read the card. Everyone, put down a token. Turn them over together. Who can say why in one sentence?
flow.kid: Read a card. Put a token down. Say why in one sentence.

ask.q: What is the difference between mass and weight in this card?
good: Mass is how much stuff there is. Weight is how hard the world pulls on it.
Mass stays the same, and weight changes with the world.

flow.parent: Accept any reason that uses the right words. A good reason for a Same card is that it depends on how much stuff, or on shape, and not on the pull. A good reason for a Different card is that it depends on how hard the world pulls or pushes.
flow.context: In this step, you play the main game and score points.

flow.do: Look at the world cards together. Pick one and a mass, and work out the weight. Check with the next world card.
flow.say: Pick a world and a mass. Multiply the mass by the number on the back of the world card. What do you get?
flow.kid: Pick a world. Pick a mass. Multiply to find the weight.

check.q: A bag has a mass of 10 kilograms. About what is its weight on Mars, where the pull is 3.7 newtons for each kilogram?
check.why: Weight is mass times the pull of the world. 10 times 3.7 is 37 newtons. Picking 98 uses the Earth's number. Picking 3.7 forgets to multiply by the mass.

flow.context: In this step, you practise working out weight from mass on another world.

flow.do: Count the points and name a winner. Then ask which kind of card was hardest.
flow.say: Who has the most points? Which kind of card was hardest, Same or Different?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which cards were hardest?
flow.think: Which of these things would be the same on any world, and which depend on how hard the world pulls?
flow.context: This is the last step of Moon Market.

experiments.title: The Rubber Band Scale: how does the stretch grow with the load?
experiments.question: If you hang more and more water from a rubber band, how does the stretch grow? Can you use the band as a scale to find the mass of something you do not know?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If 100 grams stretches the band by 1 centimetre, how far will 300 grams stretch it? Will 500 grams stretch it exactly five times as far? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same band, the same cup and the same ruler every time. Add the water 100 millilitres at a time, and wait 10 seconds before reading, because a rubber band keeps creeping. Read at eye level from the same point on the cup. Only the load changes, so any change in the stretch comes from the load.

materials.item: one wide, fresh rubber band, about 6 to 8 centimetres long when slack. A thin old band may stretch too far.
a hook, a nail, or a shelf edge to hang the band from, and some tape
a small cup or katori with three pieces of thread tied to its rim and joined in a loop, and a paper clip to hang it
a 30-centimetre ruler, taped upright behind the band
a measuring cup marked in millilitres, and a jug of water
a tray to catch spills, a notebook and a pencil
three things to weigh at the end, each between 50 and 400 grams, such as a lemon, a steel tumbler and a book. A kitchen scale to check them is useful.

experiments.safety: A rubber band under load can snap and sting, so keep your face and eyes to one side, and never load more than 500 millilitres. If anyone has a latex allergy, use a latex-free band. Stop if the band stretches to three times its slack length. Work over a tray to catch spills, and wipe the floor if water goes on it.

schedule.what: Guess. Hang the band and the cup. Add water 100 millilitres at a time and read the stretch. Draw the graph. Weigh three unknown things.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a graph with the mass in grams along the bottom and the stretch in centimetres up the side. Join the dots with a smooth line. Write the mass of each of your three unknown things.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a scale from a rubber band and water, and find how the band stretches as the load grows. Then you use it to weigh three unknown things.

setup.art: A wide rubber band hanging from a hook, with a ruler taped upright behind it and a small cup on a thread loop hanging from the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the rubber band and the cup. Tape the ruler behind them.

setup.art: A child pouring 100 millilitres of water from a measuring cup into the hanging cup, with the pointer moving down the ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Add 100 millilitres of water. Wait 10 seconds. Read the pointer.

setup.art: A graph with grams along the bottom and centimetres of stretch up the side, and a lemon hanging in the cup with a dotted line to the graph.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the graph. Then hang a lemon and read its mass from the graph.

flow.do: Show your child the band, the cup, the ruler and the water. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will hang a cup from a rubber band, and add water to it. 100 grams of water stretches the band a little. What will 300 grams do? And 500 grams? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A rubber band and a cup of water. How far will 300 grams stretch it? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will stretch that far?
good: Three times the water, so three times the stretch.
It will stretch more each time.
It will stretch less each time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say three times the water gives three times the stretch. That is a good guess, and it is called Hooke's law. The test checks whether a rubber band follows it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Band Scale. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Hang the band from a hook, a nail or a shelf edge. Tape the ruler upright behind it with its zero at the top, level with the top of the band. Hang the empty cup from the band. Read where the bottom of the band, or the paper clip, points on the ruler. Write it as the reading for no water.
flow.say: Here is the band, and here is the empty cup. Where does the pointer sit on the ruler now? That is our zero.
flow.kid: Hang the band and the cup. Tape a ruler behind them. Read the pointer.
flow.parent: Choose a pointer, such as the bottom of the paper clip, and always read the same point. The ruler must not move between readings. Read with your eye level with the pointer.

check.q: Why do we read the pointer with the empty cup hanging, before any water goes in?
options: So that the stretch is the change from the starting reading
So the cup can warm up
So the water does not spill
check.why: The stretch is how much longer the band gets because of the load. We need the reading with no load to compare with. The empty cup has a small mass, which counts as the zero.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the band and cup and read the starting position.

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of water into the cup, slowly so it does not bounce. Wait 10 seconds. Read the pointer. Write it. Repeat with another 100 millilitres, up to 500 millilitres in all. Work out the stretch each time by taking away the first reading.
flow.say: Add 100 millilitres. Wait for ten seconds. Read the pointer. Do you think the next 100 will stretch it the same amount?
flow.kid: Add 100 millilitres. Wait. Read. Write the number. Do it five times.
flow.parent: Each 100 millilitres of water has a mass of about 100 grams. A medium band stretches about 1 centimetre for each 100 grams. A thin band stretches much more, so stop earlier. The band can also creep for a while, which is why we wait. Do not worry if the steps are not exactly equal.

check.q: Why can we use 100 millilitres of water as a mass of 100 grams?
options: Because 1 millilitre of water has a mass of about 1 gram
Because water is lighter than anything else
check.why: The gram was first made to match 1 millilitre of water. So water gives you a standard mass in any kitchen. The cup has a small mass too, but we counted it as the zero.

flow.context: In this step, you add water to the cup, 100 millilitres at a time, and read the stretch each time.

flow.do: Draw the graph. Put the mass along the bottom and the stretch up the side. Mark a dot for each reading. Draw a smooth line through the dots. Ask your child what shape the line makes.
flow.say: Let's draw what happened. Grams go along the bottom. Stretch goes up the side. What shape do the dots make? Is it a straight line?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Mark a dot for each reading. What shape is it?
flow.parent: If the dots lie on a straight line through zero, then twice the load gives twice the stretch. That is Hooke's law. A rubber band often bends a little, because rubber is softer at first and stiffer later. Both results are real. A steel spring gives a straighter line.

check.q: A straight line through the zero mark means what?
options: Twice the load gives twice the stretch
The heavier loads stretch it less each time
check.why: A straight line through zero means the stretch grows evenly with the load. If the line bends, the stretch grows by different amounts each time, which is common for rubber.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the graph and look at its shape.

flow.do: Empty the cup. Put the first unknown thing in it, and wait 10 seconds. Read the stretch. On the graph, go along from that stretch to the line, then down to the grams. Write the mass. Do the same for the other two, and check them on a kitchen scale or with a printed pack mass. Then say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now use your scale. Put a lemon in the cup. How much does the band stretch? Use your graph to find its mass. Then check on a kitchen scale.
flow.kid: Put a lemon in the cup. Read the stretch. Use the graph to find its mass.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a band can work as a scale if you calibrate it with known masses. What I saw: 100 grams stretched it by 1 centimetre, and the lemon stretched it by 0.8 centimetres, so I read about 80 grams from the graph. Why: the stretch depends on the pull, so the same pull gives the same stretch. Your answers may be 10 to 20 grams out. That is normal for a rubber band.

check.q: Your scale says a tumbler has a mass of 140 grams, but a kitchen scale says 155 grams. What is the best thing to say?
options: The scale is close, and a rubber band is not very exact
The kitchen scale must be broken
check.why: A rubber band scale can be good to within about 10 percent. Here it is 15 grams out of 155, which is about 10 percent. Always check a homemade scale against something you trust.

flow.context: In this step, you use your graph to weigh three unknown things and check your answers.

experiments.title: Where Does It Balance? Finding the centre of gravity
experiments.question: Where does a flat cardboard shape balance? Can the balance point be a place where there is no cardboard at all?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Draw a dot on a paper copy of each shape where you think it will balance on a pencil tip. The shapes are a blob, a crescent and a ring. Why do you think the dot goes there?
experiments.fair_test: Cut all three shapes from the same cardboard. Hang each one from three different holes, from the same pin, using the same plumb line. Wait until the shape and the thread have stopped swinging before you mark the line. If you do this for each shape in the same way, any difference between the shapes comes from the shape.
results_table: My guess: the dot is on the shape or in the air?
Where the lines crossed: on the shape or in the air?

materials.item: a piece of cardboard from a cereal box, big enough for three shapes about 12 centimetres across
scissors, a pencil and a ruler
a pin, a long nail or a knitting needle, to hang the shapes from, held firm with tape on the edge of a table
about 40 centimetres of thread with a nut or a washer tied to the end, for the plumb line
a blunt pencil with an eraser, for balancing, and a sheet of paper
sticky tape

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the three small holes with a pin or a nail, and the child cuts the shapes with scissors. Cut away from your body. Tape any sharp pin or nail point firmly so that no one can touch it.

schedule.what: Guess. Cut three shapes. Hang each from three holes, draw the plumb lines, and find where they cross. Try to balance each shape on a pencil tip.

experiments.record: On each shape, draw three lines from the holes. Mark the crossing point with a dot. Draw each shape in your notebook with the dot, and write whether the dot is on the cardboard or in the air.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you hang three cardboard shapes from a pin and draw plumb lines on them. The lines cross at the centre of gravity, and you see where that is.

setup.art: Three cardboard shapes on a table: a map-like blob, a banana-shaped crescent and a ring, each with three small holes near the edge.
setup.caption: 1. Cut three shapes. Make three small holes near the edge of each.

setup.art: A cardboard blob hanging from a pin held on a table edge, with a thread and a nut hanging from the same pin, and a pencil marking where the thread crosses the edge.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a shape from a pin. Hang a plumb line from the same pin. Mark the thread's line.

setup.art: The ring with three pencil lines crossing in the middle of its hole, and the crescent with its lines crossing in the air outside it.
setup.caption: 3. Draw lines from three holes. Find where they cross.

flow.do: Show your child the three shapes drawn on paper. Ask them to mark with a dot where each will balance on a pencil tip, and why.
flow.say: Here are three shapes: a blob, a crescent and a ring. Where would each one balance on the tip of a pencil? Put a dot. Why there?
flow.kid: Three shapes. Where does each one balance? Put a dot. Why there?

ask.q: Why did you put the dot there?
good: In the middle of the shape.
Where there is the most cardboard.
I do not know where.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children put the dot in the middle of each shape, even for the ring, where the middle is a hole.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does It Balance. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut the three shapes from the cardboard. A grown-up makes three small holes, about as wide as a pencil lead, near the edge of each shape, spaced well apart. Tape the pin or nail so it sticks out sideways from the table edge.
flow.say: Cut out a blob, a crescent and a ring. Each gets three small holes near its edge. We will hang each shape from its holes, one at a time.
flow.kid: Cut out the three shapes. A grown-up makes three small holes in each.
flow.parent: The blob can be any rough shape, even one that looks like a map. The crescent should be quite curved. The ring should have a big hole, about half its width. The holes must be a little larger than the pin, so the shape can swing freely.
flow.context: In this step, you cut out three shapes and a grown-up makes small holes for hanging.

flow.do: Hang the blob from one hole on the pin. Hang the plumb line from the same pin. Wait until both are still. Put a dot on the shape's edge where the thread crosses it. Take the shape off, and draw a line from the hole to the dot. Do this for the other two holes.
flow.say: Hang the blob from one hole. Hang the thread beside it. When both are still, mark where the thread crosses the edge. Draw a line from the hole to the mark.
flow.kid: Hang the blob. Hang the thread. Wait. Mark the edge. Draw a line.
flow.parent: The thread must hang in front of the shape, touching it lightly. The lines from the three holes should cross at one place, or make a tiny triangle. The centre of gravity is in the middle of the tiny triangle. Now try to balance the blob on the eraser end of a pencil at that spot.

check.q: The blob hung from a pin, and the thread hung from the same pin. What does the thread show?
options: The straight line down through the shape's centre of gravity
The widest part of the shape
check.why: A hanging shape swings until its centre of gravity is directly below the pin. The plumb line also points straight down from the pin. So the line you draw passes through the centre of gravity.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the blob and draw its plumb lines.

flow.do: Do the same with the crescent, then with the ring. Draw at least two lines on each, using two or three holes. Then lay each shape on paper and trace round it. Use a ruler to extend the lines past the edges.
flow.say: Now hang the crescent. Where do you think the lines will cross? Now the ring. Where will its lines cross? Draw them and see.
flow.kid: Hang the crescent and the ring. Draw their lines. Extend them on paper.
flow.parent: For the ring, the lines cross in the middle of the hole. For the crescent, they cross in the air, in the hollow of the curve. If you draw only two lines, check with a third. Tracing on paper lets you see lines continue past the edge of the cardboard.

check.q: The lines on the ring cross in the middle of the hole. What does that tell you?
options: The ring's centre of gravity is in empty space, with no cardboard there
The pin was in the wrong place
check.why: The centre of gravity is the one point where all the pulls on all the crumbs of cardboard seem to act as one. For a ring, that point is in the empty middle. It is not a piece of the ring.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the plumb lines for the crescent and the ring.

flow.do: Try balancing each shape on a pencil tip or eraser at its crossing point. Then ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Balance each shape. Then say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: The blob balances on the pencil at the crossing point. The ring and the crescent cannot, since the point is in the air. You can balance the ring across a finger or a pencil laid under its middle, or show that it rests level on a thread stretched across the hole. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the centre of gravity is where the plumb lines cross, and it may not be on the shape. What I saw: for the ring and the crescent, the lines crossed where there was no cardboard. Why: gravity pulls on every part, and the pulls add up to one pull at a point.
flow.context: In this step, you test the balance points and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Where Does the Mass Go? Weighing before and after
experiments.question: When sugar dissolves, ice melts and a bottle fizzes, does the total mass change? If it changes, where does the mass go?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess for each test. Will the mass stay the same, go down or go up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kitchen scale on the same flat table for every weighing. Wipe the outside of each container dry before you weigh it, and wait until the number stops changing. In each test, weigh everything before and after, and change nothing else between. For the fizz test, do the closed bottle and the open cup in the same way, so the only difference is whether the gas can escape.

materials.item: a digital kitchen scale that reads in whole grams
two cups or small jars, a spoon, and 100 millilitres of water in a measuring cup
2 tablespoons of sugar
a zip-lock bag, 6 ice cubes, and a bowl of warm tap water
a strong plastic bottle from a fizzy drink, with its cap, of 500 millilitres
1 teaspoon of baking soda for the bottle and 2 teaspoons for the cup, from the kitchen
2 tablespoons of white vinegar for the bottle and 100 millilitres for the cup
a small square of tissue paper, a steel tumbler for the open test, a kitchen sink, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Baking soda and vinegar are kitchen ingredients, but vinegar stings the eyes, so keep your face away. A grown-up does the closed bottle part. Use only a strong fizzy-drink bottle, and only 1 teaspoon of baking soda in it, because the gas makes pressure. Swirl the bottle gently and do not shake it hard. Wear glasses, point the cap away from every face and open it slowly over the sink. The bath water should be warm, not hot. Never use a glass jar or a thin bag for the fizz.

schedule.what: Guess. Weigh the sugar and water before and after mixing. Weigh a sealed bag of ice before and after it melts. Weigh a closed bottle and an open cup before and after fizzing.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with the mass before, the mass after, and the change for each test. Circle any change bigger than 1 gram, because the scale only reads whole grams.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you weigh things before and after they change, to see if any mass is lost. You use sugar in water, melting ice and a fizzing bottle.

setup.art: A kitchen scale with a cup of water and a second cup of sugar beside it, and a child writing numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh the cup of water and the sugar. Add up the two numbers.

setup.art: A sealed zip-lock bag of ice cubes on the scale, then the same bag in a bowl of warm water.
setup.caption: 2. Weigh the sealed bag of ice. Melt it in warm water. Dry the bag and weigh it again.

setup.art: A capped fizzy-drink bottle on a scale, and beside it an open steel tumbler with foam, on the same scale.
setup.caption: 3. Weigh a closed bottle and an open cup before and after the fizz.

flow.do: Show your child the scale and all the things. Ask for a guess and a reason for each test. The tests are sugar in water, melting ice and fizzing. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will weigh things before and after they change. Sugar in water. Ice melting. A bottle fizzing. Will the mass stay the same, go down or go up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sugar in water. Melting ice. A fizzing bottle. Does the mass change? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the mass will change, or stay the same?
good: The sugar vanishes, so the mass goes down.
Nothing is lost, so it stays the same.
The fizz makes gas, so it goes up.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the sugar disappears and the mass goes down. A few say the fizz makes it heavier. All are good guesses to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does the Mass Go. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Weigh a cup with 100 millilitres of water in it. Write it down. Weigh the sugar in a second cup and write it down. Add the two numbers. Pour the sugar into the water and stir until it dissolves. Weigh the cup of sugar water. Compare it with the added numbers.
flow.say: Weigh the water. Weigh the sugar. Add them up. Now stir the sugar into the water. Weigh again. Has any mass gone?
flow.kid: Weigh the water. Weigh the sugar. Stir them together. Weigh again.
flow.parent: The sugar water should have the same mass as the water and sugar added up, within 1 gram. Leave the spoon in the cup the whole time, or weigh it too. Sugar seems to vanish, but every grain is still there, spread through the water as tiny pieces.

check.q: The water and the sugar added up to 250 grams. After stirring, the cup of sugar water weighs 250 grams. What does this show?
options: The sugar is still in the water. No mass was lost
check.why: Dissolving breaks the sugar into very tiny pieces spread through the water. They are still there, and still weigh the same.

flow.context: In this step, you weigh water and sugar before and after the sugar dissolves.

flow.do: Put the 6 ice cubes in the zip-lock bag and press the air out, then seal it. Dry the outside. Weigh it. Stand the bag in a bowl of warm tap water until the ice melts. Take it out, dry the outside very well, and weigh it again.
flow.say: Weigh the sealed bag with ice. Now let the ice melt in warm water. Dry the bag and weigh it again. Is it lighter, heavier or the same?
flow.kid: Seal ice in a bag. Weigh it. Let it melt. Dry the bag. Weigh it again.
flow.parent: The mass should be the same within 1 gram. The bag must be sealed and dry. If you do not dry the outside, droplets from the warm bath will make the bag seem heavier. A cold bag also attracts water from the air, so dry it just before weighing.

check.q: The sealed bag of ice has the same mass after it melts. What does this show?
options: Melting changes the ice into water, and no mass is lost
check.why: Melting changes how the particles are arranged, not how many there are or how much each one weighs. So the mass stays the same.

flow.context: In this step, you weigh a sealed bag of ice before and after it melts.

flow.do: A grown-up pours 2 tablespoons of vinegar into the bottle. Wrap 1 teaspoon of baking soda in a tissue twist and drop it in. At once, screw the cap on tight. Weigh the closed bottle. Swirl it gently until the fizzing stops. Weigh it again. Then point the cap away from every face, open it slowly over the sink, close it again, and weigh it once more.
flow.say: Weigh the closed bottle. Swirl it gently. The gas stays inside. Weigh it again. Then a grown-up opens the cap slowly and we weigh once more.
flow.kid: A grown-up closes the bottle. Weigh it. Swirl it. Weigh it again.
flow.parent: The closed bottle should weigh the same before and after the fizz, within 1 gram. The bottle will feel hard, because gas has made pressure. After the cap is opened and closed, the mass drops by about 1 gram, because some of the gas escaped. A scale that reads only whole grams may show a change of 0 or 1. If it shows 0, that is fine, because the test with the open cup shows it better.

check.q: The closed bottle weighs the same before and after the fizz, though a lot of gas appeared. What does this show?
options: The gas has mass, and none of it left the bottle
check.why: The bottle was closed, so everything stayed inside. The total mass did not change. The gas was made from the baking soda and the vinegar, and it weighs what they weighed.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes a closed fizzing bottle and you weigh it before and after.

flow.do: Put the steel tumbler on the scale. Pour in 100 millilitres of vinegar, and press the zero button if it has one. Write the mass. Add 2 teaspoons of baking soda. Watch the number as the fizz goes on. Write the lowest number when the fizzing stops. Work out the change.
flow.say: Weigh the tumbler with vinegar. Add the baking soda, and watch the number on the scale as it fizzes. What does it do?
flow.kid: Weigh the vinegar. Add the baking soda. Watch the number. Write the lowest one.
flow.parent: The mass should drop by about 2 to 4 grams as the carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air. If you press zero before adding the baking soda, the scale will show the minus change directly. Keep the tumbler on the scale all the time. The foam may rise up the sides, so leave room in the tumbler.

check.q: In the open cup, the mass went down by 3 grams. Where did the 3 grams go?
options: Into carbon dioxide gas that floated away into the air
check.why: The baking soda and vinegar made carbon dioxide. In the open cup, the gas drifted away, carrying its mass with it. Nothing disappeared. It moved.

flow.context: In this step, you weigh an open cup of vinegar as baking soda fizzes in it.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: mass is not lost when things dissolve, melt or fizz, but it can move into gas that escapes. What I saw: the sugar water, the sealed bag and the closed bottle all kept their mass, but the open cup lost about 3 grams. Why: in the open cup the gas left, and gas has mass.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: Build a Balance, and catch a cheat

materials.item: a straight 30-centimetre ruler or a thin stick, and strong thread
two small cups or steel katoris, each hung from a loop of thread, and sticky tape
a hook, a nail, or a door handle to hang the balance from
a measuring cup marked in millilitres, and a jug of water
a tomato or a lemon, and a kitchen scale to check the answer
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Hang the balance from a firm hook, and keep it away from the edge of a table. Water on the floor is slippery, so work over a tray or wipe up any spills.

schedule.what: Build the balance and make it level. Weigh a tomato against water. Then make the arms unequal and use the swap trick.

activities.record: Draw your balance. Write the mass you found for the tomato, and the mass on the kitchen scale. Write the two answers from the swap trick and their average.
activities.context: In this activity, you build a two-pan balance from a ruler and cups. You use water as a standard mass, and then catch a cheating balance with the swap trick.

setup.art: A ruler hanging by a thread from its middle, with a small cup hanging from each end on a thread loop, and the ruler level.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the ruler by its middle. Hang a cup from each end. Make it level.

setup.art: A tomato in the left cup and a child pouring water from a measuring cup into the right cup.
setup.caption: 2. Put the tomato in one cup. Add water to the other cup until the ruler is level.

setup.art: The same balance with the middle thread moved a little to one side, and the tomato on the short arm.
setup.caption: 3. Move the middle thread to make the arms unequal. Weigh the tomato on both sides.

flow.do: Show your child the ruler, the cups, the water and a tomato. Ask how many millilitres of water they think will balance the tomato, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We are going to build a balance. A tomato goes in one cup and water goes in the other. How much water will balance the tomato? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A tomato in one cup. Water in the other. How much water will balance it?

ask.q: Why do you think it will take that much?
good: The tomato is about as big as a cup of water.
The tomato is heavier than water.
I just know what a tomato feels like.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A medium tomato has a mass of about 100 to 150 grams. Remember that 1 millilitre of water has a mass of about 1 gram.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Balance. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Tie a thread loop round the middle of the ruler, and hang it from the hook. Tape a thread loop near each end, the same distance from the middle on both sides, about 12 centimetres. Hang a cup from each loop. Slide a loop a few millimetres or tape a coin on the high side until the empty balance is level.
flow.say: First we build the balance. The cups hang the same distance from the middle. We make it level with the cups empty. Why must it be level when it is empty?
flow.kid: Hang the ruler. Hang two cups. Make it level when empty.
flow.parent: The ruler hangs from a loop at its middle. The cups hang below it, which keeps it steady. If it swings too much, shorten the thread of the cups. A tiny amount of tape on the lighter side is enough to fix a small lean.

check.q: Why must the empty balance be level before we weigh anything?
options: So that level later means the two sides are equal
check.why: If the empty balance already leans, then a level balance later would not mean the two masses are equal. So we start from level.

flow.context: In this step, you build the balance and make it level.

flow.do: Put the tomato in the left cup. Pour water into the right cup, a little at a time, from the measuring cup. Stop when the ruler is level. Add up the water you poured. Check the tomato on the kitchen scale.
flow.say: Put the tomato in one cup. Pour water into the other, a little at a time, until the ruler is level. How much water balanced the tomato?
flow.kid: Tomato in one cup. Pour water in the other until it is level. How much?
flow.parent: Pour 10 millilitres at a time near the end. The water in millilitres is the tomato's mass in grams. Your answer should be within about 10 grams of the kitchen scale. A tomato is mostly water, so it makes a good test.

check.q: The tomato balanced against 120 millilitres of water. About what is its mass?
check.why: 1 millilitre of water has a mass of about 1 gram. So 120 millilitres of water has a mass of about 120 grams, and that balances the tomato. The balance compares the masses.

flow.context: In this step, you weigh a tomato against water and check it on a kitchen scale.

flow.do: Now cheat. Slide the middle thread about 2 centimetres towards the left end, so the arms are unequal. Balance the tomato in the left cup with water in the right cup. Write the water. Then swap them: the tomato in the right cup and water in the left. Write the water again. Add the two answers and halve.
flow.say: Now we make a cheating balance. The arms are unequal. Weigh the tomato once on each side. Do the two answers agree? Which one is right?
flow.kid: Make the arms unequal. Weigh the tomato on the left. Swap sides. Weigh again.
flow.parent: The two answers will be quite different, for example 90 and 150 millilitres. The true answer is between them. The average of the two, here 120, is close to the real mass. A shopkeeper who cheats with unequal arms is caught by swapping the pans. A fair balance gives the same answer both ways.

check.q: With the cheating balance, the tomato weighed 90 grams on one side and 150 grams on the other. What is the best guess for its real mass?
options: About 120 grams, the average of the two
check.why: Unequal arms make the answer too small on one side and too big on the other. When you swap the pans, the errors go in opposite directions, so the average is close to the real mass.

flow.context: In this step, you make the balance cheat and use the swap trick to catch it.

flow.do: Ask your child where this balance would work, and where a spring scale would not. Then ask for three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Would your balance work on the Moon? Would a spring scale? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Would your balance work on the Moon? Why?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a balance compares masses, so it would work on the Moon. What I saw: water in millilitres matched the tomato's mass in grams, and swapping the pans caught the cheat. Why: gravity pulls both pans in the same way, so only the masses matter.
flow.context: In this step, you think about where the balance would work.

activities.title: Feel Another World: how heavy would one kilogram be?

materials.item: two 1-litre bottles of water, each with a mass of about 1 kilogram
a carry bag with strong handles, and a smaller bag
a measuring cup marked in millilitres, a jug of water, and a 500-millilitre bottle
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Carry no more than about 3 kilograms at a time, and keep the bag close to your body. Put the heavy bag down on the floor, not on your toes. A grown-up helps with the Jupiter bag.

schedule.what: Carry a 1-kilogram bottle. Make bags that feel like 1 kilogram on the Moon, Mars, Venus and Jupiter. Compare them in your hands.

activities.record: Make a table with the world, its pull in newtons for each kilogram, and the mass you carried to match it. Write how each one felt.
activities.context: In this activity, you carry bags of water that pull on your hand the way 1 kilogram would on other worlds. You feel how weight changes while mass stays the same.

setup.art: A child holding a 1-litre bottle of water by the neck with an arm out straight.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a 1-litre bottle. This is 1 kilogram on Earth.

setup.art: A small bag with 160 millilitres of water, labelled Moon, and one with 380 millilitres, labelled Mars.
setup.caption: 2. Fill a small bag with 160 millilitres for the Moon, and one with 380 millilitres for Mars.

setup.art: A child carrying a bag with two bottles and a half-litre bottle, labelled Jupiter, with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up helps carry the Jupiter bag, 2.5 kilograms.

flow.do: Give your child a 1-litre bottle of water to hold with the arm out straight. Ask how the same bottle would feel on the Moon. Write the guess.
flow.say: This bottle has a mass of 1 kilogram. It pulls on your hand with about 10 newtons on Earth. On the Moon, would it feel heavier or lighter? How much?
flow.kid: Hold the bottle. How would it feel on the Moon? Lighter or heavier?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard as the Earth. So the bottle would feel about as heavy as a small bag of 160 millilitres of water feels on Earth.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel Another World. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 160 millilitres of water into the small bag. This pulls on your hand like 1 kilogram on the Moon. Hold it, then hold the 1-litre bottle again. Repeat with 380 millilitres for Mars and 900 millilitres for Venus.
flow.say: A bag of 160 millilitres of water is how a 1-kilogram bottle would feel on the Moon. Hold it. Then Mars, 380 millilitres. Then Venus, 900 millilitres.
flow.kid: Make a Moon bag, a Mars bag and a Venus bag. Hold each one.
flow.parent: The numbers come from the pull of each world: Moon 1.6, Mars 3.7, Venus 8.9 newtons for each kilogram, and Earth 9.8. Divide each by 9.8 to get the fraction of a kilogram. The bag does not have less matter. It is pulled less.

check.q: A 1-kilogram bag on Mars pulls on your hand like a bag of about how much on Earth?
check.why: Mars pulls about 3.7 newtons for each kilogram, and Earth about 9.8. The Mars bag feels like 3.7 divided by 9.8 of a kilogram, which is about 380 grams.

flow.context: In this step, you make bags that feel like 1 kilogram on the Moon, Mars and Venus.

flow.do: A grown-up helps. Put the two 1-litre bottles and the 500-millilitre bottle in the carry bag. This feels like 1 kilogram on Jupiter, at the cloud tops. Carry it a few steps, with a grown-up beside you. Then put it down.
flow.say: On Jupiter, a 1-kilogram bottle would feel like this bag. It is 2.5 kilograms. Carry it a few steps. Put it down. Jupiter pulls much harder than Earth.
flow.kid: A grown-up helps. Carry the Jupiter bag a few steps. Put it down.
flow.parent: The Jupiter bag is about 2.5 kilograms. Stop if it feels too heavy. For the Sun, the equivalent is 28 kilograms, which no child should carry. Ask your child what else weighs about 28 kilograms.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up helps you carry a bag that feels like 1 kilogram on Jupiter.

flow.do: Talk about what changed and what did not. Ask your child about the mass of the bottle on each world.
flow.say: On every world, the bottle has the same amount of water in it. What changed? What stayed the same?
flow.kid: On each world, what changed in the bottle? What stayed the same?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. The mass stayed the same because the bottle has the same matter. The weight changed, because each world pulls differently. On the Moon, with a sixth of the weight, bones carry less, and astronauts' bones get weaker.
flow.think: If you lived on the Moon, would your bones get stronger or weaker than on Earth? Why do you think so?
flow.context: In this step, you think about what changes from world to world, and what does not.

activities.title: How Heavy Is the Air in Our Room?

materials.item: a long measuring tape, or a long piece of string and a ruler
a calculator, a notebook and a pencil
a kitchen scale and a pump-up ball, for the optional extra

schedule.what: Guess the mass of the air in a room. Measure the room, work out its volume, and multiply by 1.2 kilograms for each cubic metre. Compare with a child and a car.

activities.record: Draw the room as a box with its length, width and height. Write the volume in cubic metres and the mass of the air in kilograms.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure a room and work out how much mass the air in it has. It shows that air, which feels like nothing, has mass.

setup.art: A child holding one end of a tape measure along the floor of a room while a parent holds the other end at the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the length and the width of the room along the floor.

setup.art: A child pointing at the ceiling with a tape or string measuring the height, with an arrow up the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the height of the room, or count the height of the door and add the rest.

setup.art: A notebook with a box drawn and numbers for length, width, height, volume and mass of air, and a calculator.
setup.caption: 3. Multiply to find the volume, and then the mass of the air.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess the mass of the air in the room. Offer choices: a packet of rice, a child, an auto-rickshaw. Write the guess down.
flow.say: The air in this room feels like nothing. But air is made of tiny particles, and they have mass. Is the air in this room as heavy as a packet of rice, a child, or an auto?
flow.kid: Guess the mass of the air in this room. A packet of rice, a child, or an auto?

ask.q: Why did you pick that one?
good: Air has almost no mass, so a packet of rice.
The room is big, so it holds a lot of air.
Air feels like nothing, so it must be nothing.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Air has mass. A cubic metre of air at room temperature has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Heavy Is the Air in Our Room. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Measure the length and the width of the room along the floor, in metres. Measure the height from the floor to the ceiling, or work it out from the height of a door. Write the three numbers.
flow.say: Let's measure the room. How long is it? How wide? How high? Write the numbers in metres.
flow.kid: Measure the length, the width and the height of the room.
flow.parent: A bedroom is often about 3 metres by 4 metres, and 2.7 metres high. Round to the nearest half metre. If you have no tape, use steps: one big step is about 1 metre for an adult and half a metre for a child.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the length, width and height of the room.

flow.do: Multiply length by width by height to get the volume in cubic metres. Then multiply the volume by 1.2 to get the mass of the air in kilograms. Write the answer.
flow.say: Length times width times height is the volume of the room. Each cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms. So how much does the air in this room weigh?
flow.kid: Length times width times height. Then times 1.2. How many kilograms?
flow.parent: For a 3 by 4 by 2.7 room, the volume is 32.4 cubic metres, and the air has a mass of about 39 kilograms. That is as much as a child of ten or eleven. A classroom can hold a few hundred kilograms of air.

check.q: A room is 3 metres long, 4 metres wide and 2.5 metres high. About what is the mass of the air in it?
check.why: The volume is 3 times 4 times 2.5, which is 30 cubic metres. Each cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms. 30 times 1.2 is 36 kilograms.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the volume of the room and the mass of its air.

flow.do: Compare the answer with a child, a bag of rice and a small car. Then tell your child that the air above every square metre of ground has a mass of about 10 tonnes.
flow.say: The air in this room has about the mass of a child. And above every square metre of ground, the air has a mass of about ten tonnes. Why are we not squashed flat?
flow.kid: The air has mass. Above every square metre is about 10 tonnes of air. Why are we not squashed?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. The air presses on us from all sides, and the fluids inside our bodies push back with the same pressure, so we are not squashed. Atmospheric scientists estimate that a small fair-weather cloud holds about 500 tonnes of water, which is reported to be about the mass of 100 elephants.
flow.think: Air pushes on you from every side, and also pushes from inside your body. What does that do to the push?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the air's mass with familiar things.

activities.title: Heavy for Its Size: same jar, different mass

materials.item: four identical clear jars or plastic bottles with lids, each about 300 millilitres
rice, salt or fine sand, flour, and cotton wool or small pieces of foam, to fill the jars
the balance from Build a Balance, or your hands
a kitchen scale in grams, to check
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Use plastic jars or bottles, not glass. Do not taste the contents, and keep flour and fine salt away from the face and eyes. Tell a grown-up first if anyone has a wheat allergy.

schedule.what: Fill four identical jars with four different things. Guess which jar has the most mass. Check by hand, on the balance, and on the scale.

activities.record: Draw the four jars. Under each, write what is in it, your guess for its mass, and its real mass in grams. Put the jars in order from the least to the most mass.
activities.context: In this activity, you fill four identical jars with different things and compare their masses. You find that the same size does not mean the same mass.

setup.art: Four identical clear jars in a row on a table, filled with cotton wool, flour, rice and salt, each with a label.
setup.caption: 1. Fill four identical jars to the top, each with a different thing.

setup.art: A child lifting two jars, one in each hand, with a puzzled face.
setup.caption: 2. Guess which has the most mass. Lift two jars at a time.

setup.art: The ruler balance with one jar in each cup, and a kitchen scale beside it showing a number.
setup.caption: 3. Check with the balance and the scale. Put the jars in order.

flow.do: Fill each jar to the top with a different thing: cotton wool, flour, rice and salt. Shake gently so they settle and add more. Put on the lids. Ask your child to guess the order from the least to the most mass. Write it down.
flow.say: Four jars of the same size. One has cotton, one flour, one rice and one salt. Which has the most mass? Which has the least? Put them in order before you test.
flow.kid: Four jars. Cotton, flour, rice, salt. Guess the order, least to most mass.

ask.q: Why did you put them in that order?
good: Cotton is soft, so it is lightest.
Salt is tiny grains, so it is packed.
They are all the same, because the jars are.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The rice, the salt and the flour will be quite different. Typical masses for a 300 millilitre jar are about 10 grams for cotton, 150 grams for flour, 230 grams for rice and 350 grams for salt, but your jars will differ.
flow.context: This is the first step of Heavy for Its Size. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Lift two jars at a time, one in each hand, with your eyes shut. Say which feels heavier. Sort the four jars from the lightest to the heaviest by feel.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Lift two jars, one in each hand. Which feels heavier? Put them in order by feel.
flow.kid: Eyes shut. Lift two jars. Which is heavier? Put all four in order.
flow.parent: Closing the eyes stops colour or size from affecting the guess. Lift each jar by the lid so the hand feels only its pull. Switch hands if it is hard to tell.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the four jars by feel.

flow.do: Check with the balance. Put two jars in the cups, one in each, and see which side goes down. Do enough pairs to put all four in order. Then weigh each on the kitchen scale and write the masses.
flow.say: Now let the balance decide. Put two jars in the cups. Which goes down? Do enough pairs to put all four in order. Then check on the scale.
flow.kid: Use the balance. Two jars at a time. Which goes down? Put all four in order.

check.q: Four jars are the same size, but their masses are different. What does this tell us?
options: Different stuff packs a different amount of mass into the same space
The jars have different weights because they were lifted differently
check.why: The jars were all the same size, so the difference comes from what is inside. Scientists call this density: how much mass is packed into a given space.

flow.context: In this step, you use the balance and the scale to put the jars in order.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the same amount of space can hold very different amounts of mass. What I saw: the cotton jar had 10 grams and the salt jar had 350 grams. Why: salt grains pack a lot of matter into the same space, and cotton is mostly air.
flow.think: A jar of salt has about 35 times the mass of a jar of cotton. How many times as much matter is in the salt jar?
flow.context: In this step, you explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

projects.title: Van Helmont's Pot: where does a plant's mass come from?

materials.item: 200 grams of dry garden soil or potting soil, dried in the sun for a day on a tray
a plastic cup or small pot with two or three small drainage holes, and a saucer
8 moong seeds, or any quick-sprouting seeds such as fenugreek, soaked overnight
a kitchen scale in grams
a sunny window sill, a jug of water, scissors, a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Use scissors with care. Wash your hands after touching soil. Do not eat the seedlings from this pot.

schedule.what: Spread the soil on a tray in the sun to dry for a day.
Weigh 200 grams of dry soil into the pot. Weigh the dry seeds. Plant them and water them.
Water the pot and see which seeds have come up.
Water the pot and measure the height of the seedlings.
Water the pot and measure the height again.
Cut the seedlings at soil level and weigh them fresh. Spread the soil and the seedlings out to dry in the sun.
Weigh the dried soil and the dried seedlings. Compare with the start.

projects.record: A table with these lines: dry soil at the start, dry seeds at the start, fresh seedlings at the end, dried seedlings at the end, dried soil at the end. Then write what changed and what did not.
projects.context: In this project, you weigh a pot of soil, grow seedlings in it with only water, and weigh everything again. You find where the mass of a plant comes from, as Jan van Helmont tried to do about 400 years ago.

setup.art: A tray of soil drying in the sun on a window sill, and a kitchen scale beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Dry the soil in the sun. Weigh 200 grams into a pot.

setup.art: A small pot with eight moong seedlings, a jug of water, and a notebook with measurements.
setup.caption: 2. Plant eight seeds. Water them. Measure the height every few days.

setup.art: A scale with a pot of dried soil weighing about the same as at the start, and a pile of cut seedlings on a plate.
setup.caption: 3. Weigh the fresh seedlings. Dry the soil and seedlings and weigh again.

flow.do: Tell your child the story of the willow in a pot. Ask where they think a plant's mass comes from. Write the guess.
flow.say: Almost 400 years ago, a man planted a small willow in a pot of soil. He gave the tree only water for five years. The tree grew heavy. Where did all that new mass come from? The soil? The water? The air?
flow.kid: A tree grows heavy in a pot. Where does its mass come from?

good: From the soil, because the roots are in it.
From the water.
From the air.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people say soil. Van Helmont found that his soil lost almost nothing.
flow.context: This is the first step of Van Helmont's Pot. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Dry the soil in the sun for a day. Weigh 200 grams into the pot. Weigh the 8 dry seeds. Write both. Plant the seeds just under the soil. Water the pot until the soil is damp. Put it on a sunny sill.
flow.say: Weigh the dry soil. Weigh the dry seeds. Write both numbers down. Plant the seeds. Water the pot. Put it in the sun.
flow.kid: Weigh the dry soil and the seeds. Plant them. Water the pot.
flow.parent: The soil must be dry at the start and dry at the end. Sun-dried soil on a tray for a day is dry enough for a kitchen scale. Seeds that weigh a few tenths of a gram may show as 0 or 1 on the scale. Just weigh all 8 together.
flow.wait: Dry the soil for a day first. Then plant.
flow.context: In this step, you weigh the dry soil and seeds and plant them.

flow.do: Water the pot a little each day, enough to keep the soil damp. On days 4, 9 and 15, look at the pot and measure the height of the tallest seedling in centimetres. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Water the pot a little every day. Measure the tallest seedling on day four, nine and fifteen. How fast is it growing?
flow.kid: Water the pot. Measure the tallest seedling. Write the height.
flow.parent: Moong seedlings grow quickly, up to 10 or 15 centimetres in two weeks. The pot needs light but not strong midday sun, which can dry it. Do not add anything to the water.
flow.wait: Water every day, and measure on days 4, 9 and 15.
flow.context: In this step, you water the pot and measure how the seedlings grow.

flow.do: On day 16, cut all the seedlings off at the soil level and weigh them together, fresh. Write the number. Pick out any big bits of root from the soil. Spread the soil and the seedlings on separate trays in the sun to dry.
flow.say: Cut the seedlings off at the soil. Weigh them fresh. Write the number. Spread the soil and the seedlings out to dry in the sun.
flow.kid: Cut the seedlings. Weigh them fresh. Spread the soil and seedlings out to dry.
flow.parent: Eight seedlings may weigh about 8 to 15 grams fresh, while the seeds weighed about 1 gram when dry. Most of that fresh mass is water. That is why you must dry them to compare fairly. The soil should dry for two days.

check.q: The seedlings weigh much more fresh than the seeds weighed dry. Where did most of the extra mass come from?
options: Water, and a little from the air
check.why: A fresh seedling is mostly water. The soil lost very little mass. Most of the extra fresh mass is water, plus a small amount of solid stuff that the seedling made from the air and water.

flow.context: In this step, you cut and weigh the fresh seedlings and start the drying.

flow.do: Weigh the dried soil and write the number. Weigh the dried seedlings and write the number. Compare the soil with the 200 grams at the start. Then say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Weigh the dried soil. Is it still about 200 grams? Weigh the dried seedlings. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Weigh the dried soil and the dried seedlings. Compare with the start.
flow.parent: Expect the dried soil to be within about 2 grams of 200. The dried seedlings will weigh about 1 or 2 grams. A kitchen scale reading in whole grams cannot show tiny changes, so do not claim too much. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the plants did not get their mass from the soil. What I saw: the soil still weighed about 200 grams, while the seedlings weighed many grams fresh. Why: the mass came mostly from water and from the air.
flow.think: Van Helmont thought it was all water. Today we know a plant's dry mass is built mostly from carbon dioxide in the air. How could you test that?
flow.context: In this step, you weigh the dried soil and seedlings and compare them with the start.

challenges.title: The Overhang Challenge: how far can a stack stick out?
challenges.problem: Stack 8 identical matchboxes, one on each layer, on the edge of a table. Make the stack stick out over the edge as far as possible without falling. Count how many box lengths the top box sticks out beyond the table.
constraints: Use 8 identical matchboxes, laid flat in the same direction, one box on each layer.
No glue, no tape and no pushing from behind. The stack must stand for 10 seconds on its own.
Measure the overhang from the table edge to the front of the top box.
Build the stack from the bottom up, or from the top down, as you like.
materials: 8 identical closed matchboxes, or 8 identical small books or blocks
a table with a straight edge, and a ruler
general: Move each box a little further out than the one below it, by the same step each time. Keep going until the stack is about to fall, and step back one.
Find the furthest step that a single box can move out before it falls, and then build the stack from that idea.
Put one big heavy thing on the back of the stack, on the table, to hold it down.
creative: Build from the top down. The top box can stick out half its length over the one below. The two top boxes together can stick out a quarter of a length over the third. Then a sixth, then an eighth. The steps get smaller, and the stack goes much further.
Add a counterweight: a second stack, or a heavy book, on the table side of the stack, to hold the back down.
Try to make the total overhang more than one whole box length with only 4 boxes.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your plan. Build it and measure the overhang in box lengths. Change one thing and try again. How far did the best stack stick out? Why do you think it stayed up?
challenges.safety: Work on the floor or a low table, so falling boxes do not hit anyone's toes. Keep small boxes away from small children who put things in their mouths.
challenges.context: This is a challenge about the centre of gravity. You stack matchboxes to stick out over the edge of a table without falling.

setup.art: Eight matchboxes stacked in an even staircase on a table edge, with the top box sticking out over the edge by about half a box.
setup.caption: 1. Build an even staircase of boxes. See how far it sticks out.

setup.art: The same boxes stacked from the top down in steps of a half, a quarter, a sixth and an eighth, with a ruler measuring the overhang.
setup.caption: 2. Build a stack with smaller and smaller steps. Measure again.

setup.art: A notebook with a drawing of the best stack and numbers, with a plumb line from the centre of gravity falling on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Draw your best stack. Show where the centre of gravity is.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to guess how many box lengths the top box can stick out with 8 boxes. Write the guess.
flow.say: You have 8 matchboxes and a table edge. How far can the top box stick out without falling? Half a box? A whole box? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Eight boxes and a table. How far can the top box stick out? Guess.

good: Half a box, or the box falls.
More than a whole box, if you are clever.
Only a little bit.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children and many adults say less than one box length. The answer for 8 boxes is more than one and a quarter box lengths.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Overhang Challenge. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Build the first stack with equal steps. Place the first box on the table, then each box a little further out than the one below. Keep going until it nearly falls. Measure the overhang and write it in box lengths.
flow.say: Build your first stack. Slide each box out a little further than the one below, by the same step. Stop before it falls. How far does it stick out?
flow.kid: Build a stack with equal steps. Measure how far it sticks out.
flow.parent: Equal steps give an overhang of about one box length with 8 boxes, or less. Write the number. This is the score to beat.
flow.context: In this step, you build a stack with equal steps and measure the overhang.

flow.do: Look at the top box alone. Ask how far it can stick out over the box below. Test it. Then add the second box, and test how far the top two together can stick out over the third box. Write the answers.
flow.say: The top box on its own can stick out half its length. The top two boxes together can stick out a quarter more. Test it. What is the pattern?
flow.kid: Test the top box. Then the top two. How far can each stick out?
flow.parent: For the top two boxes together, the centre of gravity of the pair lies halfway along them. They can stick out a quarter of a box length over the third box. Then the top three can stick out a sixth over the fourth, and so on. The steps are a half, a quarter, a sixth, an eighth.

check.q: The top box can stick out half its length over the box below. Why does it fall if it sticks out more than half?
options: Its centre of gravity moves past the edge of the box below
The box below pushes it down
check.why: A box stays up while the vertical line down from its centre of gravity falls on the box below. At half a length, the line is exactly at the edge. Any further, the line falls in the air and the box tips.

flow.context: In this step, you test how far the top box, and then the top two, can stick out.

flow.do: Build the stack from the top down. Use steps of a half, a quarter, a sixth, an eighth and so on, of a box length. Measure the total overhang in box lengths. Compare it with your first stack.
flow.say: Now use the pattern. Build from the top down. The top box sticks out a half. The next step is a quarter, then a sixth. How far does the whole stack stick out now?
flow.kid: Build from the top down. Steps of a half, a quarter, a sixth. Measure again.
flow.parent: With 8 boxes, the total overhang is half of (1 plus one half plus one third plus one quarter plus one fifth plus one sixth plus one seventh plus one eighth). That is about 1.36 box lengths. Real boxes will give a little less, because it is hard to place them exactly. Matchboxes are about 5 centimetres long, so the overhang is about 7 centimetres.

check.q: With the half, quarter, sixth pattern, the stack sticks out further than the equal-steps stack. Why?
options: Each box is placed exactly as far as its pile allows, so no box is wasted
check.why: In the equal-steps stack, some boxes are not pushed to their limit, and others have to be held back. The pattern puts each step at the limit set by the centre of gravity of the boxes above.

flow.context: In this step, you build the smarter stack from the top down and measure the overhang.

flow.do: Compare the stacks. Ask where the centre of gravity of the whole stack lies, and why the stack does not fall.
flow.say: Which stack stuck out the furthest? Where is the centre of gravity of the whole stack? Why does it not fall?
flow.kid: Which stack won? Where is its centre of gravity? Why does it stay up?
flow.parent: The centre of gravity of the whole stack must lie over the table. The overhang looks as if it should fall, but the boxes on the table side hold the balance. A good answer is that the whole stack, taken as one thing, has its centre of gravity above the table.
flow.context: In this step, you compare your stacks and explain why they stay up.

videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it says the stretch grows with the load up to a limit, and shows a graph.
