videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it shows a plumb line or a balance and explains the centre of gravity as one point for all the weight.

videos.title: How the Earth was weighed: the Cavendish experiment
videos.why: To see the two lead balls and the twisting wire that Cavendish used to find the density of the Earth.
videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it describes the torsion balance and the result of about 5.4 times the density of water, and does not say Cavendish weighed the Earth directly on a scale.

quiz.p: A shopkeeper's two-pan balance holds a mango and a 300-gram weight, and the pans are level on Earth. On the Moon, what will the pans do?
opts: Stay level
The mango side will go down
The weight side will go down
quiz.why: A balance compares two masses. The Moon pulls both pans by the same fraction, so they stay level.

quiz.p: A spring scale shows 6 newtons for a bag on Earth. About what will it show on the Moon?
opts: About 1 newton
About 6 newtons
About 36 newtons
quiz.why: The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard, so the scale shows about one sixth of 6, which is 1 newton. The bag's mass has not changed.

quiz.p: A steel spring stretches 3 centimetres under 300 grams. What does Hooke's law say about 600 grams?
opts: It stretches about 6 centimetres
It stretches about 3 centimetres
It stretches about 9 centimetres
quiz.why: Twice the load gives twice the stretch, until the elastic limit. Twice 3 centimetres is 6 centimetres.

quiz.p: You hang known masses on a rubber band, and the line on your graph bends. What is the best thing to say?
opts: The band is not perfectly even, so use the graph to read masses, and do not assume equal steps
The experiment has failed and must be thrown away
The band follows Hooke's law exactly
quiz.why: Rubber bands often give a curved line. The graph still works as a scale if you read masses from it, because you calibrated it with known masses.

quiz.p: A child has a mass of 20 kilograms. On Mars the pull is 3.7 newtons for each kilogram. What is her weight there?
opts: 74 newtons
20 newtons
7.4 newtons
quiz.why: Weight is mass times the pull: 20 times 3.7 is 74 newtons. Picking 20 forgets the pull. Picking 7.4 loses a zero.

quiz.p: Which of these is the same on every world?
opts: The mass of a bag of rice
The weight of the bag of rice
The reading of a spring scale
quiz.why: Mass is how much matter there is, and the bag carries all of it everywhere. Weight and a spring scale's reading depend on the pull of the world.

quiz.p: The plumb lines drawn on a cardboard ring cross in the middle of its hole. Where is the ring's centre of gravity?
opts: In the hole, where there is no cardboard
On the cardboard nearest the pin
It has no centre of gravity
quiz.why: The pulls on all the crumbs of cardboard act as one pull at the crossing point, and for a ring, that is in the empty middle.

quiz.p: A bus with luggage piled on its roof topples more easily on a sharp bend than an empty bus. Why?
opts: The luggage raises the centre of gravity, so a smaller tilt takes its line outside the wheels
The luggage makes the bus weigh less
The luggage pushes the bus off the road
quiz.why: The higher the centre of gravity, the sooner the line down from it leaves the base. Low, wide and heavy-at-the-bottom is stable.

quiz.p: A bottle of vinegar and baking soda is sealed and weighed before and after it fizzes. Then the same fizz is done in an open cup. What is the result?
opts: The sealed bottle keeps its mass, and the open cup loses some, as gas floats away
Both keep their mass exactly
Both lose mass
quiz.why: Gas has mass. In the sealed bottle, it cannot leave. In the open cup, it floats away and the scale shows a drop.

quiz.p: Sugar is stirred into a cup of water until it cannot be seen. What happens to the mass of the cup and its contents?
opts: It stays the same
It goes down, because the sugar has gone
It goes up, because the sugar is wet
quiz.why: Dissolving breaks the sugar into tiny pieces that spread through the water. They are still there and still weigh the same.

quiz.p: What did Cavendish's number for the Earth's density, about 5.4 times that of water, show?
opts: The inside of the Earth is denser than the rocks at the surface
The Earth is made of water
The Earth is lighter than the Moon
quiz.why: Surface rock is only about 2.7 times as dense as water. A much bigger average means a much denser inside, which we now know is an iron core.

quiz.p: A litre of water has a mass of about how much?
opts: 1 kilogram
100 grams
10 kilograms
quiz.why: The litre and the kilogram were first meant to match. A litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram, so water is a handy standard mass.

quiz.p: A homemade scale and a trusted scale give different answers for the same tomato. What should you do first?
opts: Check both against a known mass, such as a litre of water
Trust the homemade scale, because you made it
Trust the shiny one, because it was dearer
quiz.why: Before you trust any scale, weigh something you already know. The one that disagrees with the known mass needs fixing.

items.p: A shopkeeper in Coimbatore balances a mango against a 250-gram weight on a two-pan balance, and the pans are level. The balance and both things are taken to the Moon. What happens?
opts: The pans stay level, because both pans are pulled less by the same amount
The mango side goes down, because it is heavier
The weight side goes down, because iron is heavy
items.why: A balance compares two masses, and the Moon pulls both pans by the same fraction. So the pans stay level. The mango still has a mass of 250 grams on the Moon.

items.p: On Earth, the weight of a bag with a mass of 1 kilogram is about ____ newtons.
items.why: Earth pulls with about 9.8 newtons for each kilogram. For quick sums, 10 is close enough.

items.p: A spring scale gives the same reading for a mango on the Moon as on the Earth.
items.why: False. A spring scale measures the pull on the mango, and the Moon pulls about six times less. So the scale would show about one sixth of the Earth reading.

items.p: 100 millilitres of water has a mass of about how much?
opts: 100 grams
10 grams
1 kilogram
items.why: 1 millilitre of water has a mass of about 1 gram, so 100 millilitres has a mass of about 100 grams. This is why water is a handy standard mass in any kitchen.

items.p: Sort these. Would each one be the same on the Moon, or different?
items: the mass of a bag of rice
the weight of that bag of rice
the number of grains in the bag
the reading of a spring scale
the reading of a two-pan balance
the stretch of a rubber band under a stone
items.a: see items
items.why: Mass, counting and a balance's answer depend on how much stuff there is. Weight, a spring scale and a rubber band's stretch depend on how hard the world pulls.

items.p: Match each tool to what it does.
pairs: Measures a pull by the stretch of a spring
Gives a standard mass of about 1 kilogram
Senses a push in a digital scale
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool uses a different idea. A balance uses comparison, a spring scale uses stretch, a plumb line shows where gravity points, water gives a handy standard, and a strain gauge senses a tiny bend.

items.p: Put these steps in order for finding the mass of a tomato with a rubber band scale.
items: Hang the tomato and read its stretch
Read the tomato's mass from the graph
Add known masses of water and read the stretch each time
Hang the empty cup and read the zero
Draw the graph of stretch against mass
a: Hang the empty cup and read the zero
Add known masses of water and read the stretch each time
Draw the graph of stretch against mass
Hang the tomato and read its stretch
Read the tomato's mass from the graph
items.why: First find the zero, then calibrate with known masses, then draw the graph, and only then use it for an unknown mass.

items.p: On the Moon, the pull is about 1.6 newtons for each kilogram. About what is the weight of a bag of 5 kilograms on the Moon?
opts: About 8 newtons
About 49 newtons
About 5 newtons
items.why: Weight is mass times the pull: 5 times 1.6 is 8 newtons. Picking 49 uses the Earth's number. Picking 5 forgets to multiply.

items.p: The centre of gravity of a thing is always inside the thing.
items.why: False. For a ring, it is in the empty hole. For a crescent or a banana, it is in the air beside the shape.

items.p: A plumb line, a weight on a thread, always points straight ____.
items.why: Gravity pulls the weight straight down, towards the centre of the Earth, and the thread follows that line.

items.p: Explain why a two-pan balance gives the same answer on the Moon as on the Earth.
items.a: A balance compares two masses. On each pan, the world pulls down. If the masses are equal, the pulls are equal wherever you are, so the pans stay level. The balance never measures how hard the world pulls.
items.why: A strong answer says that both pans are pulled by the same world in the same way, so only the masses matter.

items.p: Why does a spring scale show a smaller number for the same mango on the Moon?
items.a: A spring scale measures the pull on the mango, which is its weight. The Moon pulls about six times less than the Earth, so the spring stretches less. The mango has the same mass, but a smaller weight.
items.why: A strong answer separates mass, which stays the same, from weight, which is the pull and changes with the world.

items.p: Draw a cardboard ring hanging from a pin. Draw a plumb line down from the pin, and mark where the centre of gravity is.
items.a: The ring hangs from the pin at its top. The plumb line is a straight vertical line down from the pin, through the empty hole. The centre of gravity is a dot on that line in the middle of the hole.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the dot in the hole, not on the cardboard, and the line straight down from the pin.
items.art: A blank box with a pin drawn at the top and space to draw a ring, a thread with a nut hanging from the pin, and a dot.

items.p: Label this drawing of a two-pan balance: beam, left pan, right pan, pointer, standard mass.
items.a: The beam is the bar across the top. The left pan holds the mango and the right pan holds the standard mass. The pointer is the needle in the middle that points at the mark when the pans are level. The standard mass is the iron weight in the right pan.
items.why: A balance has a beam with two pans of equal reach, a pointer to show when it is level, and a known mass to compare with.
items.art: A brass two-pan balance with a mango on the left pan and an iron weight on the right, with five blank label lines.

items.p: A steel bucket and a tall thin vase both stand on a table. Why is the bucket much harder to knock over?
opts: It has a wide base and a low centre of gravity
It is made of steel, which is heavier than glass
It is closer to the table
items.why: A thing topples when the line down from its centre of gravity passes the edge of its base. A wide base and a low centre of gravity make you tilt it much further first.

items.p: A cup holds 200 grams of water and 20 grams of sugar. The sugar is stirred in until it cannot be seen. What does the scale show for the whole cup, ignoring the cup itself?
opts: 220 grams
200 grams
180 grams
items.why: Dissolving breaks the sugar into tiny pieces, but they are still there. No mass is lost, so the total is 200 plus 20, which is 220 grams.

items.p: Look at the graph of Aarav's rubber band. For each extra 100 grams, the stretch grew by 0.9, then 1.0, then 1.1, then 1.3, then 1.5 centimetres. What does this tell you?
opts: The band does not follow Hooke's law exactly, because each extra 100 grams stretched it a bit more than the one before
The band is broken
A rubber band is the same as a steel spring
items.why: For a perfect spring, every 100 grams would add the same stretch. These steps grow, so the dots curve upwards. Rubber bands often behave like this, which is why you must calibrate them.

items.p: If you pull a spring past its elastic limit, it goes back to its old length when you let go.
items.why: False. Past the elastic limit, the spring stays stretched, and a scale made from it is spoilt.

items.p: A bag with a mass of 1 kilogram on Mars would pull on your hand like about ____ grams on Earth.
items.why: Mars pulls with about 3.7 newtons for each kilogram, and Earth with 9.8. 3.7 divided by 9.8 is about 0.38 of a kilogram.

items.p: Three of these would show a different reading on the Moon. Which one would show the same?
opts: A spring scale
A bathroom scale
A two-pan balance
A hanging forcemeter
items.why: The spring scale, the bathroom scale and the forcemeter all feel a pull or a push. The balance only compares masses, so its answer does not change.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one make a thing more stable, or easier to topple?
items: piling luggage on the roof of a bus
putting heavy sacks at the bottom of a cart
items.a: see items
items.why: A thing is stable when it must be tilted a long way before the line down from its centre of gravity leaves the base. Wide and low helps. Tall and top-heavy does not.

items.p: Put these steps in order for finding a centre of gravity with plumb lines.
items: Draw a line from the hole to the mark where the thread crosses the edge
Hang the shape from the pin by one hole
Hang the plumb line from the same pin
Do the same from two more holes
a: Hang the shape from the pin by one hole
Hang the plumb line from the same pin
Draw a line from the hole to the mark where the thread crosses the edge
Do the same from two more holes
items.why: The shape swings until its centre of gravity is below the pin, and the plumb line marks that vertical line. Doing it from several holes gives several lines that cross at the centre of gravity.

items.p: The plumb lines drawn on a cardboard crescent cross in the air beside it. What does this tell you?
opts: The centre of gravity is outside the crescent, in the hollow of its curve
The crescent has no weight
The plumb line was crooked
items.why: The pulls on all the crumbs of cardboard add up to one pull at the point where the lines cross. For a crescent, that point is in the empty hollow.

items.p: Two girls each have a mass of 30 kilograms. One stands on the Earth, where the pull is 9.8 newtons for each kilogram. The other stands on Mars, where it is 3.7. Work out the weight of each, and say what stays the same.
items.a: On Earth: 30 times 9.8 is 294 newtons. On Mars: 30 times 3.7 is 111 newtons. Each girl has a mass of 30 kilograms, which stays the same on both worlds. Only the weight changes.
items.why: A strong answer multiplies the mass by each pull, and says that mass is the amount of matter and does not change.

items.p: A sealed bottle of vinegar and baking soda weighs the same before and after it fizzes. The same mixture in an open cup weighs 3 grams less afterwards. Why?
opts: In the open cup, the gas that was made floated away, taking its mass with it
Baking soda has no mass
The open cup is lighter than the bottle
items.why: The fizz makes carbon dioxide gas, which has mass. In the closed bottle it stays in, so the total is the same. In the open cup, the gas escapes.

items.p: Match each idea to a thing you could see or do.
pairs: A Thanjavur dancing doll rocks and stands up again
A sealed bottle weighs the same before and after the fizz
A paper clip pulled open too far stays bent
A litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram
A loaded cart is harder to stop than an empty one
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each idea shows up in an everyday thing. The doll's weight is low in its base, so it rights itself. Sealed containers keep their mass. Bent clips pass the elastic limit. Water gives a standard. A bigger mass resists a change in movement more.

items.p: Surface rock is about 2.7 times as dense as water, and the whole Earth is about 5.4 times as dense. What does this tell us?
opts: The inside of the Earth must be much denser than the rock at the surface
The Earth is hollow
The surface rock is lighter than water
items.why: If the Earth were rock all the way through, its average density would be about 2.7. It is twice that, so the inside is made of something much heavier. We now know it is an iron core.

items.p: A person carrying a heavy pot of water on one hip leans to the other side. Why?
items.a: The pot pulls the combined centre of gravity of the person and the pot towards the pot's side. Leaning the other way moves it back over the feet. If they did not lean, the line down from the combined centre of gravity would fall outside their feet and they would tip.
items.why: A strong answer talks about the combined centre of gravity of the person and the load, and the line down from it staying over the feet.

items.p: A cheap digital kitchen scale shows 960 grams for a litre bottle of water. What would you do to check it, and what would you conclude?
items.a: A litre of water has a mass of about 1,000 grams, so the scale is reading about 40 grams low. I would check it with another known mass or a balance. If they agree with each other and not with the scale, the scale is wrong and needs setting right.
items.why: A strong answer uses the litre of water as a known mass, and makes a clear conclusion about the scale.

items.p: Three friends argue about the centre of gravity of a cardboard ring.

views.says: It has to be in the cardboard, because that is where the weight is.
It is in the hole. The weight of all the cardboard acts as if it were at the middle.
There is no such thing. It is just a point we make up to add up all the pulls.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use something from this unit as evidence. Then say what another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer usually agrees with Farhan, because the plumb lines crossed in the empty hole. It admits that Meera has a point: the centre of gravity is a point that we work out by adding up the pulls, and is not a piece of the cardboard. Asha's idea does not fit what the lines showed.
items.why: There is a real argument here. Engineers sometimes say it is only a calculation. A strong answer uses the plumb-line evidence and is fair to the idea that it is a worked-out point.

items.p: Draw a bucket tilted halfway over on the floor. Draw the line straight down from its centre of gravity, and show whether it will tip back or fall over.
items.a: The bucket is tilted on one bottom edge. The vertical line from the centre of gravity falls inside that edge, so the bucket tips back. If the line fell outside the edge, it would fall over.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the line from the centre of gravity and where it falls compared with the edge on the floor.
items.art: A blank box with a floor line and a steel bucket tilted on one bottom edge.

items.p: A kilogram of cotton wool and a kilogram of iron balance each other on a two-pan balance.
items.why: True. A balance compares masses, and both have a mass of 1 kilogram. The cotton takes up far more room, but that does not matter to a balance.

items.p: A lorry piled high with sacks is more likely to topple on a sharp bend than the same lorry with the sacks low. Why?
opts: The high load raises the centre of gravity, so a smaller tilt takes its line outside the wheels
The sacks are heavier when they are high
The wheels grip less when the load is high
items.why: The same load weighs the same wherever it is. But a higher centre of gravity means the line down from it leaves the base after a smaller tilt, so the lorry topples more easily.

items.p: A steel spring stretches 2 centimetres under a 200-gram load. If it follows Hooke's law, how far will it stretch under 500 grams?
opts: 5 centimetres
4 centimetres
10 centimetres
items.why: Twice the load gives twice the stretch, and 500 grams is 2.5 times 200 grams. So the stretch is 2.5 times 2, which is 5 centimetres.

items.p: A bag has a mass of 12 kilograms. Work out its weight on Earth (9.8 newtons for each kilogram), on the Moon (1.6) and at the cloud tops of Jupiter (25). Show your working.
items.a: On Earth: 12 times 9.8 is 117.6 newtons. On the Moon: 12 times 1.6 is 19.2 newtons. On Jupiter: 12 times 25 is 300 newtons. The mass is 12 kilograms in every place.
items.why: A strong answer multiplies the mass by the pull each time, shows each step, and keeps the mass at 12 kilograms.

items.p: On which world would a 1-kilogram bag pull on your hand like a bag of 160 grams does on Earth?
opts: The Moon
Mars
Jupiter
items.why: The Moon pulls with about 1.6 newtons for each kilogram. That is 1.6 divided by 9.8, which is about 0.16 of a kilogram, or 160 grams. Mars would be 380 grams, and Jupiter 2.5 kilograms.

items.p: The Earth and the Moon both circle a point that is inside the Earth.
items.why: True. The balance point of the Earth and the Moon is about 4,700 kilometres from the Earth's centre. The Earth's radius is about 6,400 kilometres, so the point is inside the Earth.

items.p: A tall narrow wardrobe and a low wide one have the same mass. Why is the tall narrow one easier to tip over?
items.a: The tall one has a higher centre of gravity and a narrower base. You only need to tilt it a little before the line down from its centre of gravity falls outside its base. The low wide one needs a much bigger tilt.
items.why: A strong answer uses the line down from the centre of gravity and the edge of the base.

items.p: The top box of a stack can stick out half its length over the box below, but no further. Why not?
opts: Further out, the line down from its centre of gravity would fall in the air, and it would tip
The box below pushes it back
The table edge is sharp
items.why: A box stays up while the line down from its centre of gravity falls on the box below. At half a box length, the line is at the edge of that box.

items.p: A litre of water has a mass of about ____ kilogram.
items.why: The litre and the kilogram were first made to match. A litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram, which is why water is a handy standard.

items.p: A sealed bag of ice is weighed, then the ice melts in warm water, and the bag is dried and weighed again. What will the second weighing show?
opts: The same mass as the first
Less mass, because ice is heavier than water
More mass, because water is heavier than ice
items.why: Melting changes how the particles are arranged, not how many there are. In a sealed bag, nothing can leave, so the mass is the same.

items.p: The air in a room is 4 metres long, 5 metres wide and 3 metres high. A cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms. What is the mass of the air in the room? Show your working.
items.a: The volume is 4 times 5 times 3, which is 60 cubic metres. 60 times 1.2 is 72 kilograms. The air in the room has a mass of about 72 kilograms, about as much as a grown-up.
items.why: A strong answer works out the volume first, then multiplies by 1.2, and compares the answer with something familiar.

items.p: Three traders at a market argue about how to weigh pepper.

views.says: A digital scale is quicker and easier to read, so it is better.
A balance with iron weights cannot be fooled by a weak battery, and it works anywhere.
Both are fine if they are checked against a standard mass, such as a litre of water, every day.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use something from this unit as evidence. Then say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For example, it might agree with Selvi: any scale can go wrong, and a known mass checks it, as the litre of water showed in the story. It admits Lakshmi's point that a balance only compares masses and so does not depend on a battery or on the pull of the world, and Ravi's point that a digital scale is quick.
items.why: There is a real choice here. A strong answer uses the idea of calibration and the difference between comparing and sensing a push or pull, and is fair to the other views.

items.p: Draw the Earth and the Moon, and mark the point they both circle. Show where that point is.
items.a: The Earth is a big circle, and the Moon is a small circle far to one side. A dot is marked on the line between them, inside the Earth's circle, nearer the Earth's edge than its centre.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the dot on the line between the two, and inside the Earth, because the Earth is much heavier than the Moon.
items.art: A blank box with space to draw a large Earth, a small Moon and the line between them.

items.p: Label this cut-away drawing of the Earth: crust, mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core.
items.a: The crust is the thin outer layer. The mantle is the thick rocky layer beneath it. The liquid outer core is the shell of melted iron and nickel. The solid inner core is the small ball in the middle.
items.why: The Earth's layers get denser towards the middle. The core, mostly iron and nickel, holds about a third of the Earth's mass.
items.art: A cut-away Earth with four layers shown by different shades and four blank label lines.

items.p: Henry Cavendish found that the Earth is about 5.4 times as dense as water. Rocks at the surface are about 2.7 times as dense. What followed from this?
opts: The inside of the Earth must be made of something much denser than rock
The surface rocks must be wrong
The Earth has no inside
items.why: If the whole Earth were like the surface rock, its average density would be about 2.7. The much larger number means the inside is denser, and we now know there is a core of iron and nickel.

items.p: A plant in a pot gains 10 grams of fresh mass in two weeks, while the soil in the pot barely changes in mass. Where did the plant's new mass come from?
items.a: Mostly from water that was added, and from carbon dioxide in the air that the leaves took in. A little may come from minerals in the soil, but the soil's mass barely changed. A fresh plant is mostly water.
items.why: A strong answer names water and air, and notes that the soil's mass stayed about the same.

items.p: Big G, the number that sets the strength of gravity between two masses, has been measured so exactly that all laboratories agree.
items.why: False. Different careful laboratories get answers that differ by more than they should. Big G is known to only about five digits.

items.p: A student weighs a candle before and after burning it for ten minutes in an open room and finds it lighter. Which is the best explanation?
opts: The wax turned into carbon dioxide and water vapour, which floated away
The candle lost its weight into the flame as heat
Wax has no mass when it is hot
items.why: Burning joins the wax with oxygen from the air to make invisible gases. In an open room, they float away, and the candle looks lighter. If the burning were done in a sealed jar, the total mass would stay the same.

applications: Shops and markets weigh rice, pepper and gold on balances and scales that government inspectors check against standard masses.
Hospitals and anganwadis weigh babies on digital scales, and check them with known masses so the readings can be trusted.
Lorries, buses and cranes are loaded so that their centre of gravity stays low and over the wheels, to keep them from toppling.
ISRO engineers balance a rocket so that its centre of gravity stays on the line of its engines' push, and they weigh every part.
Ships carry heavy ballast low in the hull, to keep the centre of gravity low and the ship from rolling over.
Gymnasts, tightrope walkers and high jumpers move their bodies to control where their centre of gravity is.
Geologists use tiny changes in the pull of gravity to find heavy ore under the ground and light caves.
Jewellers and pharmacists use balances that can weigh thousandths of a gram, by comparing with very small standard masses.
Bathroom and kitchen scales use strain gauges to sense a push, and show kilograms by assuming the Earth's pull.
Weighbridges at toll plazas use strain gauges to weigh whole lorries, so overloaded ones do not damage roads and bridges.

open_questions.q: Why is big G so hard to measure?
open_questions.why_open: Different careful laboratories get answers that differ by more than they should. Nobody knows if the cause is hidden mistakes, or something new about gravity.

open_questions.q: How heavy is a neutrino, the lightest known particle with mass?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show it has a mass, but only a limit on how big it can be. Nobody has measured the exact number.

open_questions.q: What is the Earth's core made of, besides iron and nickel?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think it holds a little of some lighter elements, such as sulfur, oxygen, silicon or carbon, but they cannot agree which.

open_questions.q: Why is there more matter than antimatter in the universe?
open_questions.why_open: The early universe should have made equal amounts, and they would have wiped each other out. Something left a little matter over. Nobody knows what.

open_questions.q: Does the Earth's solid inner core turn at a different rate from the rest of the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Earthquake waves hint at tiny changes in how the inner core turns, but scientists are still arguing about what they mean.

open_questions.q: Could a future kind of scale weigh single atoms with no spring or standard at all?
open_questions.why_open: The new kilogram is tied to a fixed number in nature. Scientists are working on ways to count atoms and so weigh small things directly, but it is not yet an everyday tool.

maths.problem: Aarav hung known masses on a rubber band. The pointer read 14.0 centimetres with no water, and then 14.9, 15.9, 17.0, 18.3 and 19.8 centimetres after each extra 100 grams. How much did the band stretch with 500 grams? How much more did the last 100 grams stretch it than the first 100 grams?
maths.answer: With 500 grams it stretched 5.8 centimetres. The last 100 grams stretched it 0.6 centimetres more than the first.
maths.explain: 19.8 minus 14.0 is 5.8. The first 100 grams stretched it 14.9 minus 14.0, which is 0.9. The last 100 grams stretched it 19.8 minus 18.3, which is 1.5. 1.5 minus 0.9 is 0.6.
maths.context: This is about the Rubber Band Scale test, where masses of water were hung on a rubber band.
maths.why_maths: Taking each reading from the zero gives the stretch, and comparing steps shows whether the band stretches evenly.

maths.problem: A child has a mass of 40 kilograms. The pull is 9.8 newtons for each kilogram on Earth, 3.7 on Mars and 1.6 on the Moon. Round the Earth's number to 10. Work out her weight on each world.
maths.answer: About 400 newtons on Earth, 148 newtons on Mars and 64 newtons on the Moon.
maths.explain: On Earth, 40 times 10 is 400. On Mars, 40 times 3.7: 40 times 3 is 120, and 40 times 0.7 is 28, so 148. On the Moon, 40 times 1.6: 40 times 1 is 40, and 40 times 0.6 is 24, so 64.
maths.why_maths: Weight is mass times the pull of a world, so multiplying lets you find weights on worlds you cannot visit.

maths.problem: A room is 3 metres long, 4 metres wide and 2.5 metres high. Each cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms. What is the mass of the air in the room?
maths.explain: The volume is 3 times 4 times 2.5. 3 times 4 is 12. 12 times 2.5 is 30 cubic metres. 30 times 1.2 is 36 kilograms.
maths.context: This is about the How Heavy Is the Air in Our Room activity, where you measured a room.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the three lengths gives the volume, and multiplying by the mass of each cubic metre turns volume into mass.

maths.problem: In the Overhang Challenge, the top box sticks out one half of a box length over the one below. The top two boxes together stick out one quarter more, the top three one sixth more, and the top four one eighth more. Add the four steps. Is the total more than one whole box length?
maths.answer: The total is 25 twenty-fourths of a box length, which is one whole box length and one twenty-fourth more. Yes, it is a little more than one whole box length.
maths.explain: Use twenty-fourths. One half is 12 twenty-fourths. A quarter is 6. A sixth is 4. An eighth is 3. 12 plus 6 plus 4 plus 3 is 25 twenty-fourths, which is one whole and one twenty-fourth more.
maths.context: This is about the Overhang Challenge, where boxes are stacked to stick out over a table edge.
maths.why_maths: Adding the steps shows that four boxes can stick out more than one whole box, which is hard to believe until you add them up.

maths.problem: On the home-made balance, a tomato balanced 120 millilitres of water and a lemon balanced 85 millilitres. Water has a mass of 1 gram for each millilitre. What is the total mass of the two? How many grams more is the tomato than the lemon?
maths.answer: Together they have a mass of 205 grams. The tomato has 35 grams more.
maths.explain: 120 plus 85 is 205 grams. 120 minus 85 is 35 grams.
maths.context: This is about the Build a Balance activity, where water was poured to balance a tomato.
maths.why_maths: Water gives a standard mass in millilitres and grams, so a balance turns any amount of matter into a number you can add and compare.

maths.problem: With the cheating balance, a tomato weighed 90 grams on one side and 150 grams after swapping the pans. What is the average of the two? Why is the average a good guess for the real mass?
maths.answer: The average is 120 grams. It is a good guess because the cheat makes one answer too small and the other too big, by about the same amount.
maths.explain: 90 plus 150 is 240. Half of 240 is 120. The unequal arms made the first answer 30 too low and the second 30 too high, so they cancel out.
maths.context: This is about the swap trick in the Build a Balance activity.
maths.why_maths: Averaging two readings that err in opposite directions cancels most of the error, which is how swapping the pans catches a cheat.

maths.problem: A 1-kilogram bag on Mars feels like 380 grams on Earth. How many grams on Earth would a 3-kilogram bag on Mars feel like? How many litres of water is that?
maths.explain: The bag has 3 times the mass, so it pulls 3 times as hard. 3 times 380 is 1,140 grams. Water has 1 gram for each millilitre, so 1,140 grams is 1,140 millilitres, which is 1.14 litres.
maths.context: This is about the Feel Another World activity, where bags of water matched the pull of other worlds.
maths.why_maths: Doubling or tripling the mass doubles or triples the weight on every world, so one measurement lets you scale up to any bag.

maths.problem: A closed bottle weighed 612 grams before and 612 grams after fizzing. An open cup weighed 612 grams before and 608 grams after. A second open cup lost 3 grams. How much gas escaped from the first cup? Which cup lost more, and by how much?
maths.answer: 4 grams escaped from the first cup. It lost 1 gram more than the second cup.
maths.explain: 612 minus 608 is 4 grams. The second cup lost 3 grams. 4 minus 3 is 1, so the first cup lost 1 gram more. The closed bottle lost nothing, because the gas stayed in.
maths.context: This is about the Where Does the Mass Go test, where bottles and cups were weighed before and after fizzing.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the mass before and after shows exactly how much gas escaped, because the loss in mass is the mass of the gas.

maths.problem: The average density of the Earth is 5.5 grams for each cubic centimetre. Granite is 2.7 grams and water is 1 gram. About how many times as dense as granite is the Earth? How many times as dense as water?
maths.answer: About 2 times as dense as granite, and 5.5 times as dense as water.
maths.explain: 5.5 divided by 1 is 5.5. 5.5 divided by 2.7 is a bit more than 2, because 2 times 2.7 is 5.4. So the Earth is about twice as dense as granite.
maths.why_maths: Estimating the ratio shows how much denser the Earth is than its surface rock, which is why Cavendish's number told us about the core.

roots.context: We have hung cardboard shapes from a plumb line and weighed things two ways. Now we ask what the centre of gravity tells us about things, about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: Every crumb of the cardboard ring was pulled down by the Earth. Yet the whole ring acted as if one single pull worked at its centre. At that centre, there is only a hole. So the place where a thing's weight seems to act can be a place with nothing in it.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the weight is in the thing', or 'the middle of it is the heaviest part', as if weight sat inside the material. But weight is a pull on every part, and the one place where it all seems to act is a point that we work out.
deep_truth.evidence: In Where Does It Balance, the plumb lines for the ring crossed in the empty hole, and the lines for the crescent crossed in the air beside it. There was no cardboard at either place.

three.who_am_i: Your balance point is somewhere near your belly when you stand. When you bend over, it can move out into the air in front of you, and you keep your balance by moving your feet.
three.what_is_life: Every standing animal, including you, stays up by keeping the balance point above the feet. Walking is falling forwards and catching yourself again.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth and the Moon circle a balance point that is inside the Earth. The Sun and Jupiter circle a balance point that is just outside the Sun, in empty space.

roots.thread: Gravity pulls on every particle of a thing, one by one. Yet all of those separate pulls add up to something that behaves like a single pull at a single place. The same trick works for the Earth, the Moon and the Sun: many pulls from many particles can be treated as one pull from one point. The balance point is not a thing. It is the place where all the small pulls agree.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes share one hub, but it is the empty space in the middle that makes the wheel useful. Clay is shaped into a pot, but it is the emptiness inside that holds what you pour in.
teachings.link: The centre of a ring is a hole, yet it is the place where the whole ring's weight seems to act. The empty middle is what the whole shape turns on.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Indra's net is a net of jewels in which every jewel reflects every other jewel. Each one holds all the others.
teachings.link: Every particle of the Earth pulls every particle of the cardboard ring, and each of them pulls back. The balance point is where all those separate pulls meet and agree.

science.text: The weight of any object acts as if it were one force through its centre of gravity. For a ring, a crescent or a person bending over, that point can lie outside the object.
The balance point of the Sun and Jupiter lies just outside the surface of the Sun, in empty space.

other_view.view: The centre of gravity is only a calculation: an average of where the mass is, weighted by how much there is. Calling it the place where the weight acts is a handy shortcut. Nothing special is going on at that point, and it is no more a thing than the average height of a class.

practice.title: Find your balance
practice.say: Stand with your feet together and your arms by your sides. Breathe slowly three times. Now lift one foot a little, and feel your body shift over the other foot. Lift your arms out to the sides, and feel how that steadies you. Put the foot down. Where is your balance point right now, and what is holding it above your feet?
practice.kid: Stand on both feet. Slowly lift one foot. Feel your body shift over the other foot. Arms out helps. Where is your balance?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: water is the standard mass everywhere in the unit, because 100 millilitres of water has a mass of about 100 grams, so a family with a measuring cup has a set of weights. The Rubber Band Scale needs a wide, fresh band and never more than 500 millilitres of water, with a safety line about snapping and the face kept to one side. Real bands vary a lot, so the unit tells the parent to expect about 1 centimetre for each 100 grams from a medium band, a curved line from many bands, and answers 10 to 20 grams out. Where Does It Balance uses cereal box cardboard and three cut shapes, with a grown-up making the holes. The ring's lines cross in the hole and the crescent's in the air, which is checked by tracing the shape on paper and extending the lines. Where Does the Mass Go needs a scale that reads whole grams. The sugar and ice tests should change by 1 gram or less. The closed bottle test uses only 1 teaspoon of baking soda and 2 tablespoons of vinegar in a strong fizzy-drink bottle, done by a grown-up, and the cap is opened slowly over the sink. The open cup should lose about 2 to 4 grams. The Overhang Challenge uses matchboxes. The half, quarter, sixth and eighth steps give about 1.36 box lengths with 8 boxes, and real boxes give a little less. Van Helmont's Pot takes 18 days, and a kitchen scale cannot show the plants' small dry mass, so the unit says the test shows only that the soil lost very little compared with what the plants gained fresh. Facts to verify before publishing: the typical box and jar masses in Heavy for Its Size, which depend on the jars. The Earth and Moon balance point distance of about 4,700 kilometres (checked); the date of van Helmont's experiment (given as the first half of the 1600s). The value of Cavendish's density, about 5.4. And the Thanjavur dancing doll as a low-centre-of-gravity toy. The spine is the Rubber Band Scale, the explanation cards, Where Does It Balance, roots and the quiz.

how_we_found_out.story: By the 1700s, people could measure how hard the Earth pulls, but not how much the Earth weighs. Isaac Newton had said that a mountain might pull a plumb line a little sideways. In 1774, Nevil Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal in England, measured how much a mountain in Scotland pulled a plumb line sideways. The pull was tiny, but it gave a first answer. In 1798, Henry Cavendish used a device built by John Michell, who had died. Two small lead balls hung from a rod on a thin wire. Two big lead balls were brought close. Every mass pulls every other mass, so the wire twisted a very little. From the twist, Cavendish found that the Earth is about 5.4 times as dense as water. Rocks at the surface are only about 2.7 times as dense. So the Earth could not be rock all the way through. Something much heavier had to be deep inside.
how_we_found_out.who: Henry Cavendish, an English scientist (1731 to 1810)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Earth is rock all the way through, so its average density is that of surface rock, about 2.7 times water. Cavendish's number, about 5.4, showed that the inside must be much denser. Later work found an iron core.
